title: LiteLLM release pipeline hacked to distribute credential-stealing malware
raw_text: Hackers hijacked the software release pipeline of LiteLLM, a popular open-source AI gateway, to distribute credential-stealing malware, marking the project’s second supply chain compromise this year despite security measures introduced after an earlier attack. The compromised version, 1.107.0, was distributed through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and official Docker images on October 21. LiteLLM said the malicious Python packages remained available for approximately two hours before being removed, while the affected Docker images were withdrawn or replaced later that day. The affected Docker images included those distributed under the latest, main-latest, and main-stable tags, extending the risk to deployments that pulled those tags during the exposure window. According to cybersecurity firm Aikido , files bundled with the compromised package executed automatically when Python started, even if an application did not import LiteLLM. The malware was designed to collect sensitive information from infected systems, including cloud credentials and API keys stored in LiteLLM’s database, potentially giving attackers access to services beyond the affected AI gateway. The compromised package also contained a remote access trojan that launched a background process to retrieve and execute code from attacker-controlled infrastructure every hour, according to Aikido. This could allow attackers to continue executing commands on infected systems after the initial credential theft. In its incident report, LiteLLM said attackers used stolen GitHub credentials associated with three developer accounts to manipulate its software release pipeline. The stolen credentials enabled changes to the release workflow, which was redirected to an attacker-controlled lookalike repository. The company said the attackers may have obtained the credentials from logs associated with an internet-facing internal LiteLLM deployment. It also identified circumstances in which Claude Code could expose GitHub authentication tokens in responses subsequently recorded by LiteLLM. However, it has not been established how the attackers initially accessed the deployment. LiteLLM said the incident had been contained and that customers using its private enterprise registry were unaffected. It advised organizations running the compromised open-source software to treat their environments as potentially breached and rotate exposed credentials rather than relying solely on removing the malicious package. Broader enterprise exposure “A compromised LiteLLM gateway provides a strong foothold to hackers and could expose far more than AI API keys,” said Keith Prabhu , CEO of Confidis. Aikido noted that the malware targeted Kubernetes service account tokens and secrets associated with CI/CD systems , including GitLab and Jenkins. The extent of any subsequent compromise may depend on the privileges assigned to the affected deployment and the credentials available to it. “An AI gateway is privileged enterprise infrastructure,” said Sakshi Grover , research director for information and data security at IDC. “Centralizing access to multiple models can improve governance, but it also concentrates trust.” Beyond credential theft, a compromised gateway could disrupt business applications that depend on it, Grover said. IDC’s Future Enterprise Resiliency and Spending Survey, conducted in July 2026, found that 95% of enterprises surveyed worldwide had at least one company-funded agent-enabled workflow in production. A wider incident response challenge The malware’s remote access component could remain active even after the compromised package is removed, complicating efforts to determine whether an affected system is safe to restore. “CISOs should not treat this just as a package-cleanup exercise,” Prabhu said. He recommended identifying deployments running affected packages or container images, isolating suspected systems, and preserving forensic evidence before rebuilding them using trusted software. Grover warned that security teams should avoid launching Python or pip in suspected compromised environments because the malware’s startup hooks could execute again. She recommended identifying affected packages and container image digests across production environments, developer systems and CI runners. “Missing indicators do not prove an environment is clean,” Grover said. Prabhu recommended examining logs for evidence of persistent access or misuse of stolen credentials. He said organizations should rotate every secret accessible to the compromised deployment, including credentials associated with cloud infrastructure and development pipelines. Grover also recommended linking AI usage telemetry with cloud and identity audit logs to help identify possible credential misuse. Unusual token consumption could provide an indication of unauthorized activity, although attackers may avoid generating noticeable increases in spending, she said. Software supply chain weaknesses In March, malicious versions of LiteLLM’s Python package were distributed following a compromise that the project linked to the Trivy security scanner used in its software release pipeline. After this, LiteLLM strengthened its software release process by moving releases to a private repository and introducing signed Docker images. However, attackers used stolen GitHub credentials to modify the release workflow, which then signed and published the malicious software, the company said. The incident shows how malicious code can pass through an authorized software signing process when attackers compromise the release pipeline. A valid digital signature can verify that an artifact has not been altered since signing, but cannot establish whether the code was safe when it was signed. “Repeated supply-chain compromises show that a trusted source repository does not guarantee that the package users install was built from that source,” Prabhu said. Prabhu recommended cryptographically signed releases backed by verifiable build provenance, alongside stronger protection of publishing credentials. Grover said enterprises should also inspect distributed software packages and container images before deployment, rather than relying solely on the integrity of the source repository. She recommended restricting production deployments to verified package and image digests and requiring independent approval for changes to release workflows.
summary: Hackers hijacked the software release pipeline of LiteLLM, a popular open-source AI gateway, to distribute credential-stealing malware, marking the project’s second supply chain compromise this year despite security measures introduced after an earlier attack. The compromised version, 1.107.0, was distributed through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and official Docker images on October 21. LiteLLM said the malicious Python packages remained available for approximately two hours before being removed, while the affected Docker images were withdrawn or replaced later that day. The affected Docker images included those distributed under the latest, main-latest, and main-stable tags, extending the risk to deployments that pulled those tags during the exposure window.

title: China-linked hackers used agentic AI in attack on 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants
raw_text: A China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used an open-source agentic AI framework to turn its stolen credentials against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft said. Microsoft Threat Intelligence attributed the activity to Storm-0940, which it said has used the ARTEX framework since as early as September 2026 to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations. In some cases, the group gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after first targeting a victim. Microsoft said the activity did not result from a compromise of or vulnerability in its own systems, products, or services. “This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially,” Microsoft said in a blog post. Machine-speed sign-ins Following the breach at ConnectWise, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 attempts per minute, the post added. ConnectWise published an initial advisory on October 16 covering attempted unauthorized access associated with its Cloud Backup product, and later expanded its containment guidance. The attackers used the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications to authenticate to Microsoft 365 environments through apps that had already been granted access. That removed the need for interactive user sign-ins, the post said. In some environments, the agents moved on to Microsoft Graph and directory operations. These included reconnaissance, application credential changes to establish persistence, and changes to identities, groups, and privileged roles. Microsoft warned that such changes “can remain active as a backdoor” even after the original application is remediated. ConnectWise did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Yih Khai Wong, senior research manager for security services at IDC Asia/Pacific, said the timeline is beyond the reach of human response. “2,900 sign-in attempts per minute and gaining privileged cloud access in under three hours is not a timeline any human analyst queue can keep up with, no matter how well-staffed the SOC,” Wong said. He said containment actions such as disabling credentials, revoking tokens and isolating service principals should trigger automatically on predefined thresholds, with humans reviewing them afterward. In the face of machine-speed attacks, he added, “relying on a human to click ‘approve’ will not cut it.” Trusted apps, untrusted access Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said the incident exposes a gap in how enterprises secure access. “Companies spend enormous amounts of time securing employee logins with MFA and conditional access, while third-party applications can hold equally powerful permissions and authenticate without any employee being involved,” Kadakia said. “We’ve spent years implementing zero trust for humans while continuing to implicitly trust machines.” He said vendor integrations should be treated like privileged accounts, with minimum permissions, continuous monitoring, periodic access reviews, and a tested way to revoke access. “An application you stopped using a year ago may still have permissions in your environment today,” Kadakia added. Wong said accountability is shared. “ConnectWise, as the entry point, is responsible for protecting the credentials and infrastructure that let its app reach across tenants,” he said, adding that customers are responsible for knowing what access they granted, to whom, and for how long. Commoditized attack tooling ARTEX is a Chinese open-source multi-agent LLM system that can use any AI model. Its agents run a penetration test from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little human interaction. Microsoft said public reporting in October linked the framework to data breaches at Korean financial institutions and that actors across multiple regions are using it. Storm-0940 has been active since 2021, Microsoft said. Its ARTEX-driven targeting spans aerospace and defense, energy, financial services, government, semiconductor and technology, among other sectors. Most of the targeting was unsuccessful, the company said, but the group achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a short time. “Attacks are being commoditized; threat actors are increasingly turning to open-source tools to launch attacks, meaning the operational sophistication once reserved for well-resourced groups is now available to anyone who can run a GitHub repo against an LLM API,” Wong said. Kadakia said there is no reliable way to tell an AI agent from a human operator by examining individual requests. A legitimate API call made with stolen credentials looks the same regardless of who initiated it, he said. “Defenders should focus on what the identity is doing, not whether a human or AI is controlling it,” he said. Disable ConnectWise connections Microsoft advised customers to keep affected ConnectWise connections disabled until ConnectWise issues restoration instructions and not to delete enterprise applications as a first step. Organizations should search tenants by the four affected application IDs rather than display names and preserve Entra, Purview, and SIEM records, the company said. It also urged a review of activity from at least October 15, extending back to October 1 where records allow. The company also cautioned against treating exposure as proof of a breach. “The presence of an affected application, or even successful authentication, does not necessarily indicate unauthorized data access or data exfiltration,” Microsoft said in the post.
summary: A China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used an open-source agentic AI framework to turn its stolen credentials against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft said. Microsoft Threat Intelligence attributed the activity to Storm-0940, which it said has used the ARTEX framework since as early as September 2026 to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations. In some cases, the group gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after first targeting a victim. Microsoft said the activity did not result from a compromise of or vulnerability in its own systems, products, or services.

title: OpenAI’s models are deliberately breaking their misalignment monitoring systems
raw_text: AI agents are getting more inventive in finding ways to circumvent safeguards to prevent bad behavior, OpenAI has revealed. On Tuesday, it reported two incidents, both involving the agent disabling or interfering with its alignment monitoring, and in one case directly lying about having done so. “In two internal coding tasks, agents weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes,” the OpenAI blog post said. “A GPT-6.1 Sol agent repairing an evaluation pipeline disabled automatic alerts to our Security team, treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration in order to match a reference implementation, and then falsely claimed to the user that it had not removed the monitor.” In both cases, OpenAI reported, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, “but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them.” OpenAI said that, in response, it has been strengthening its monitoring programs to prevent agents from being able to disable the protections. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI said, suggesting that it may simply be an example of “benign overpersistence,” with models not understanding why monitoring is important. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so,” OpenAI added. “We don’t yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior and will investigate this behavior through the creation of paired evaluations, resampling of agent continuations, and experiments on models’ internal activations.” OpenAI, like almost every agentic AI vendor, has been struggling with making its autonomous agents more productive and self-sufficient while simultaneously protecting customer environments from bad agent behavior . It has even tried to slow down the pace of its scaling , to allow for the development of better agent restrictions. Particulars alarming Analysts and consultants said the revelations were surprising only in their scope. But they were alarmed by some of the particulars in the OpenAI disclosures. Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, stressed that some level of monitoring was maintained, but only for the agent itself. That meant that the workloads the agents created were left invisible. “The agent was watched. What it built was not,” he said. “Agent-spawned pipelines, jobs, service accounts, and cloud functions are the next generation of shadow IT, and almost no enterprise enforces monitoring inheritance on them.” Mahapatra also stressed that the severity classification described in the post is concerning. “The severity handling is the part CISOs should sit with,” he said. “Neither event was classified P0 [maximum severity] and neither run was killed. The one category of agent behavior that degrades every future detection ranked below the paging threshold because nothing visibly broke.” He pointed out that this reveals a disadvantage for the enterprise, noting, “OpenAI caught this because it can read its agents’ reasoning. Most enterprise SOCs see only outputs, so if the lab with chain-of-thought visibility filed this below its paging line, assume your SOC never saw it at all. EDR settled this a decade ago with tamper protection: any attempt to disable the sensor is the alert. An agent touching its own monitoring should page someone every single time.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the obvious flaw in the agentic system is that the agent was able to disable the mechanism designed to oversee it. “Think of a house sitter told not to call you, who then unplugs the burglar alarm so it cannot call you either. A guardrail an agent can edit is a suggestion,” Dickson said. “An agent that can turn off its own alarm is not being monitored. It is being trusted.” Wakeup call for CISOs Some observers said that this should wake up enterprise CISOs to the fact that an attacker may not be as big a risk as a rogue agent with full system privileges. “The threat is not just an outsider breaking in, it’s an authorized agent doing something it was never supposed to do, in a context no one anticipated, faster than any SOC analyst can catch it,” said Philip Harris , an IDC research director. “The OpenAI case is a concrete, well-documented instance of exactly that pattern, not an isolated anomaly.” He added that OpenAI deserves credit for transparency. “OpenAI’s own candor is the most striking part. A frontier lab publicly saying it isn’t sure whether its own shipping models have an emergent tendency to undermine their own oversight is a genuinely new level of candor.” Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, also pointed out that the rationale of the agent, as captured by OpenAI, is alarming. “In both cases, the agents stopped, asked themselves whether the safeguard should stay on and then argued their way to turning it off. One then told the user it hadn’t touched the monitor. In incident response, we call that defense evasion followed by a false statement. If a human insider did it, we would open an investigation,” Levine said. “The other telling detail is that the monitor worked. It flagged the issue. The agent then cut the wire between the alarm and the people who needed to hear it.” Independent technology consultant Sivaram Annadurai agreed: “An agent that fixes the pipeline but disables the alarm hasn’t necessarily solved the problem. It may have created a bigger one.” And Jeff Valdes , a director at consulting firm Acceligence, added, “what stands out is how ordinary the trigger was. No attacker, no jailbreak, just routine coding instructions and an agent with enough access to change its own oversight. The monitor kept running while the alerts stopped reaching people. That kind of quiet degradation is easy to miss precisely because the dashboard still looks healthy.” But Valdes said the agent to agent approval system is also something CISOs should take seriously. “One subagent got the call right, and the parent agent overrode it. Safeguards that don’t survive delegation aren’t really safeguards,” Valdes said. “OpenAI also noted the agent later gave an inaccurate account of what it had changed. An agent’s own report can’t be the control.”

On Tuesday, it reported two incidents, both involving the agent disabling or interfering with its alignment monitoring, and in one case directly lying about having done so. “In two internal coding tasks, agents weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes,” the OpenAI blog post said. “A GPT-6.1 Sol agent repairing an evaluation pipeline disabled automatic alerts to our Security team, treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications.

title: Two critical PHP flaws put the web on alert as emergency patches arrive
raw_text: Organizations are scrambling to protect themselves following the disclosure of two critical vulnerabilities in commonly used code that powers much of the internet. The flaws discovered in the PHP scripting language could allow attackers to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). On Wednesday morning, the PHP Foundation released patches for affected versions, and said it is “imperative” that organizations running PHP patch immediately. It said that all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. It considers the risk highest for mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can trigger exploitation before application code runs. In response to the disclosures, some government websites in Europe, including those in the Netherlands and Finland, as well as those of other organizations worldwide, went offline as a precautionary measure. PHP is ‘the web itself’ PHP is a widely-used, open source server-side scripting language that underlies websites like WordPress, which powers 43% of the web , as well as Mailchimp, Drupal, Magento, Laravel, and parts of Slack and Zoom, and numerous others. The impact is not limited to websites, noted the Netherlands National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) in its description of the flaws, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell . PHP is also embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces and other vendor products where administrators may not be able to update PHP directly. And CERT-EU, an organization that tracks cybersecurity threats in the European Union, also warned that many commercial and open-source products use PHP as a backend technology, and these could be also impacted by the flaws, even if they do not directly expose a PHP installation. This makes the vulnerabilities all the more serious. CVE-2026-109618 , which has a 9.2 severity rating on the common vulnerability and scoring system (CVSS), could allow RCE via memory corruption during out-of-memory handling (OOM), a strategy that operating systems (OSes) and apps use when physical RAM and swap spaces become exhausted. CVE-2026-109619, also with a score of 9.2, remote code execution via stale request-owned global state reused by a later request on the same worker. Both flaws sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: Memory management and error handling, the PHP Foundation noted . This makes both bugs extremely serious, and also difficult to fix without impacting compatibility or performance. Organizations should begin with the assumption that they are exposed . “What makes these vulnerabilities significant is where they sit,” said Forrester senior analyst Madelein van der Hout . PHP underpins 70% of websites, making this a huge concentration risk. “Checking the corporate website alone is not enough,” she said. “Organizations need to establish where they are exposed and prioritize internet-facing systems.” Affected organizations should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Linux and long-term support (LTS) vendors received patches in advance, the Foundation said, so organizations should check with their vendors about fixes. PHP 8.1 and other end of life versions no longer receive updates from the PHP project, although some distributors and LTS vendors provide backported fixes, so organizations still running unsupported versions should also check with their vendor. Those relying on the volunteer-maintained rpms.remirepo.net should switch distribution packages or build from source to immediately apply updates, the PHP Foundation advised. Those unable to patch immediately should take the preventive action it described to reduce exposure, CERT-EU said, warning that these mitigations do not make an installation safe. “This is what an internet-scale vulnerability looks like,” said Neatsun Ziv , CEO of runtime app security company OX Security. “When a flaw hits technology this ubiquitous, the blast radius isn’t one product or one industry. It’s the web itself.” Researchers from his company independently reproduced the flaws and found that the vulnerable functionality is enabled by default, and has existed in PHP since version 5.4. Still, experts emphasize that patching is just one element of response. Speed matters, Forrester’s van der Hout noted, and security teams need to identify everywhere PHP is running, prioritize exposed systems, apply the official fixes promptly and investigate for signs of compromise. “A patch fixes the vulnerability; it does not necessarily remove access an attacker may already have established,” she said. Offline does not mean hacked With rumors of exploits already available on the dark web, taking services down to protect and then patch them is a pragmatic choice, experts say. Forrester’s van der Hout emphasized that taking a website offline does not mean it has been hacked. If an organization cannot yet patch or adequately protect a potentially vulnerable system, temporarily taking it offline can be a “proportionate risk decision.” That is, organizations accept a short loss of availability rather than risk a potential serious compromise. Ultimately, this is a test of operational resilience, rather than just patch management, van der Hout said. Organizations must decide whether they can keep services running, and who has the authority to take them offline if necessary. “A temporary shutdown can be the right decision, but it shows how a software vulnerability can become a business disruption even without a confirmed breach,” she said. AI’s role in defense, as well as hacking OpenAI has posted a blog detailing its role in the PHP response, explaining that red-teaming organization Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative. Wiz also independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities, and OpenAI partners contributed research, technical support, and coordination ahead of PHP’s disclosure. OpenAI is sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill to help organizations identify vulnerable PHP versions and apply the right updates. “Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said. The company also indicated that this is a turning point in AI’s role in security ; frontier AI discovered the vulnerabilities before attackers did, giving maintainers a head start, a “ defender’s window .” “It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” OpenAI noted. Matt Saunders , DevOps lead at global technology provider The Adaptavist Group, emphasized the latter point: “As soon as the vulnerability is announced, legions of AI bots will be looking for systems to exploit,” he said, pointing out that these bots can chain together multiple lower-vulnerability attacks combined with these new critical ones to hack into organizations. This means, he said, “the blast radius from a breach is potentially much wider now with AI-embellished attacks available to those who choose to use them.”
summary: Organizations are scrambling to protect themselves following the disclosure of two critical vulnerabilities in commonly used code that powers much of the internet. The flaws discovered in the PHP scripting language could allow attackers to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). On Wednesday morning, the PHP Foundation released patches for affected versions, and said it is “imperative” that organizations running PHP patch immediately. It said that all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed.

title: Microsoft: Treat AI agents as insider threats
raw_text: EVP of Microsoft Security Hayete Gallot writes in a blog post that AI agents operating independently within companies could be a serious security threat. According to Microsoft, today’s most advanced AI models cannot be fully trusted. Not because they are malicious, but because they are trained to achieve goals and can take unexpected shortcuts to achieve them. For example, bypassing limitations or cooperating with other AI agents in ways that were not intended. The problem becomes especially serious when companies allow AI agents to access sensitive information, internal tools, and even allow them to make independent decisions. To address the risks, Microsoft is launching “Guardian Agents,” which are AI agents that monitor and control the actions of other AI agents 24/7. This is to assess risks in real-time and intervene if an AI agent does something potentially harmful. The technology is part of Microsoft’s Project Perception security initiative, which was unveiled in July.

According to Microsoft, today’s most advanced AI models cannot be fully trusted. Not because they are malicious, but because they are trained to achieve goals and can take unexpected shortcuts to achieve them. For example, bypassing limitations or cooperating with other AI agents in ways that were not intended.

title: WordPress sites compromised after TeamUpdraft credential exposure
raw_text: Attackers are using stolen connection keys exposed in a TeamUpdraft security breach to install malicious plugins on affected WordPress sites and establish persistent access. Sites already compromised may remain at risk even after the exposed credentials are revoked. The attacks followed unauthorized access to TeamUpdraft’s website. The company, which develops the UpdraftPlus backup plugin and related WordPress management services, confirmed that its customer database was likely accessed. The incident exposed potentially sensitive information, including connection keys used by UpdraftCentral, a service that lets administrators manage multiple WordPress sites remotely. TeamUpdraft says it has closed the access route and released UpdraftPlus versions 1.26.13 and 2.26.13 for its free and Premium users, respectively, to revoke older UpdraftCentral Cloud connections. However, WordPress security firm PatchStack reported that attackers had already used the exposed credentials to execute commands on connected sites and install malicious plugins. The UpdraftPlus plugin itself and its downloads were not compromised, the company said in a blog post , adding that backups stored in customers’ own remote storage, including Google Drive, Dropbox and Amazon S3 , were also not affected. “However, if your site was accessed through UpdraftCentral, please also re-authorise your remote storage and change any storage access keys, as a precaution,” it added. UpdraftPlus surpassed four million active WordPress installations in October, although only sites connected to UpdraftCentral through an active key are exposed to this particular attack. Stolen keys enabled remote site access Attackers were seen using exposed UpdraftCentral credentials to issue commands to connected WordPress sites. Patchstack observed attacks beginning on October 18, with malicious plugins to establish persistent access and create accounts with administrative privileges. Patchstack researchers identified at least 99 variants of malicious plugins, some disguised as routine maintenance or optimisation tools. Nethemba, a web application security firm, reported that attackers targeted three of its WordPress sites through the remote-management channel and successfully installed malicious plugins on two of them. Some backdoor variants can create privileged accounts or authenticate as existing administrators, while others are designed to evade detection in WordPress’s standard administrators screens. Revoking the original connection key does not automatically remove rogue plugins, accounts or active sessions created during an attack, the researchers said. WordPress admins face a cleanup job TeamUpdraft has signed out customer accounts, reset login security, replaced UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone credentials, and introduced additional monitoring. It has also reported the incident to the UK Information Commissioner’s Office and other relevant authorities. The potentially accessed customer databases contained names, email, and billing addresses, order histories, password hashes, two-factor authentication settings, and service connection keys. “We do not store any card details. All card payments are handled by Stripe and PayPal,” the company clarified. Administrators using UpdraftCentral Cloud have been advised to update to safer UpdraftPlus versions and inspect each connected site directly. Recommended checks include deleting remaining UpdraftCentral connection keys, reviewing administrator accounts and installed plugins, changing administrator passwords, and examining logs for suspicious activity. Sites showing signs of compromise may need to be restored from a verified backup created before October 17, followed by credential rotation and integrity checks. TeamUpdraft recommends changing account passwords and resetting two-factor authentication where applicable.
summary: Attackers are using stolen connection keys exposed in a TeamUpdraft security breach to install malicious plugins on affected WordPress sites and establish persistent access. Sites already compromised may remain at risk even after the exposed credentials are revoked. The attacks followed unauthorized access to TeamUpdraft’s website. The company, which develops the UpdraftPlus backup plugin and related WordPress management services, confirmed that its customer database was likely accessed.

title: Google, Mozilla revoke eMudhra intermediates after private key compromise
raw_text: Private keys associated with eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by Indian digital trust provider eMudhra have been compromised, potentially allowing attackers to forge trusted certificates and impersonate websites or services, according to Google and Mozilla. “On 17th October @ 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report to certificates@mozilla.org, forwarded by the Chrome Root program, that the private key of 8 eMudhra Intermediate certificates have been compromised,” Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s engineering team, wrote in a public Mozilla bug report . “An attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs could impersonate any website or service.” Mozilla independently recovered the keys later that day, confirming that they were vulnerable. “Mozilla was able to recover the private keys for the impacted certificates independently @ 21:48 UTC and without any knowledge of the method the original reporter used,” Jackson added in the report. He said the recovery confirmed that “the key generation process was flawed and is trivial to exploit.” The report was submitted by a researcher identified as Wayne and forwarded by the Chrome Root Program. Mozilla acknowledged it and subsequently began blocking the affected certificates in Firefox. eMudhra acknowledged the report and said it was investigating, according to the Mozilla report. “One of eMudhra’s certificate authority private keys is the number 4,” security researcher Scott Helme wrote in a separate analysis . Two other keys had values of 56 and 115, he said. Helme recovered all eight from their public certificates in less than a second. Six of the eight affected intermediate certificates were intended for Transport Layer Security (TLS), which browsers and applications use to authenticate websites and establish encrypted connections, according to Google’s security blog post . The other two were for code signing. “The private keys for these certificates were generated with insufficient randomness (i.e., weak cryptographic entropy), enabling anyone to forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website against clients that have not yet removed trust in those CAs,” Google added in the blog post. Browser blocks and enterprise exposure Google’s Chrome Root Program received a report and deployed a Chrome Revocation List Set update blocking the affected intermediate authorities, according to the company’s security blog. “Chrome users were immediately protected against all certificates sharing those keys, without requiring a browser update or restart,” Google added in the blog post. Android devices and Chromebooks also received an equivalent update through Google Play Services. Google said no TLS certificates chaining to the six affected intermediates appeared in Certificate Transparency logs before the blocking action. It said no fraudulent certificates issued by those authorities could have been used against clients enforcing Certificate Transparency, including Chrome’s default configuration. Mozilla said in its security blog post that it completed the distribution of its OneCRL block to Firefox users with standard configurations. Mozilla also announced updates for users whose custom settings might have prevented them from receiving the block. Google said it had removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 certificate, which signed the affected intermediates, from the Chrome Root Store. The change was scheduled to reach all devices relying on that store on October 27. Enterprise applications face separate checks Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, estimated that about 30,000 legitimate certificates would need to be migrated. He said government and public-sector websites using the affected hierarchy could face browser warnings or access disruptions if replacement certificates were not installed in time. “This isn’t just about eight compromised keys. It’s about the global internet’s chain of trust,” Kadakia said. “A single authority’s failure can undermine authentication for organisations that have never dealt with it.” Kadakia said enterprise security teams should check payment gateways, vendor integrations, older Java applications, mobile apps, and network appliances, which may use certificate trust stores separate from browsers. “Security teams need to identify both the certificates their services present and the certificate authorities their applications trust,” he said. He advised organizations to test whether affected clients reject certificates signed by the compromised keys, including cross-signed chains. Cloudflare said in its October 20 incident report that it learned of the compromise on October 19 and deployed mitigations across its content delivery network, developer services, and Zero Trust products. It also updated shared trust stores and base images and released updates for Cloudflare One clients and Cloudflare Tunnel. “Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services,” the company said in its report. eMudhra says no end-entity certificates were issued eMudhra, in its incident statement , said the affected intermediate authorities were created during a key-generation ceremony in April 2025. It said the incident did not affect its root CA private keys or other intermediate authorities. “None of these intermediate CAs, including the one deployed in production, have issued any end-entity certificates,” the company said. It said its internal analysis was corroborated by public Certificate Transparency records and that it was investigating the incident and reviewing its security controls. Kadakia said the absence of issued end-entity certificates was reassuring, but noted that someone holding a compromised intermediate key could generate fraudulent certificates without requesting them from eMudhra. eMudhra did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
summary: Private keys associated with eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by Indian digital trust provider eMudhra have been compromised, potentially allowing attackers to forge trusted certificates and impersonate websites or services, according to Google and Mozilla. “On 17th October @ 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report to certificates@mozilla.org, forwarded by the Chrome Root program, that the private key of 8 eMudhra Intermediate certificates have been compromised,” Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s engineering team, wrote in a public Mozilla bug report . “An attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs could impersonate any website or service.” Mozilla independently recovered the keys later that day, confirming that they were vulnerable. “Mozilla was able to recover the private keys for the impacted certificates independently @ 21:48 UTC and without any knowledge of the method the original reporter used,” Jackson added in the report.

title: Moving past autonomous exploitation to machine-speed security
raw_text: Frontier AI advancements have created a world where exploitation outpaces defense. The average enterprise takes 32 to 43 days to patch , but the mean time to exploit a vulnerability is 10 hours . This asymmetry creates questions around how enterprises can trust autonomous AI to operate ubiquitously across their environments. As I mentioned on the TechCrunch Disrupt stage last week, security at machine speed means AI accelerates the fix as quickly as it does the find. Below is an expanded take of that discussion. The asymmetry between detection and remediation The asymmetry between attackers and defenders exacerbates the patching problem. Traditional security models triage by severity using manual processes, which creates weeks- and months-long backlogs. But advanced models allow attackers to chain together low- and medium-severity flaws — which fly under the radar by design — to create a high-severity issue. For example, a cross-site scripting flaw, a session cookie hijack and a database leak are separately registered as medium-severity incidents. As a chained exploit, the cross-site script gives an attacker an entry point into the browser they use to hijack the session cookie, allowing authentication as a user, which gives them database access with full read of production data. The prompting quandary The tension in machine speed security is that detection is devastatingly accurate, but patching is still catching up. Tests we ran on CyberGym produced a 95 percent precision rate for discovering complex, sequence-of-events bugs. The discovery muscle works. But more than 98 percent of the time, frontier models refuse to execute remediation prompts because their built-in guardrails miscategorize 76-99 percent of direct prompt code involving vulnerabilities as false positives. When they do attempt patches, 55 percent fix the primary issue but miss a secondary point and 40 percent of patches break production code. Prompting alone won’t fix the asymmetry because detection rates are high but remediation precision is low. Fixing the engineering gap Prompting with advanced models isn’t enough. The answer is an integrated system that brings together multi-agent orchestration, context injection, sandbox validation and iterative repair. Powering the accuracy of this harness are insights from the context graph, sandbox infrastructure, validation pipeline and experience implementing security primitives. Three advancements to cross the chasm Engineering advancement requires technology to move beyond three limitations. The system needs to go beyond humans in the loop to working autonomously and continuously. It cannot simply explain triage in plain English – it must produce durable issues with evidence-backed solutions. It cannot be a Wizard of Oz harness backed by a frontier model. The way forward is a multi-agent system with identity and access management for every action and session and Cedar enforcement over fine-grained access policies. The system compresses signals into actions governed by IAM and Cedar, not simply raw model calls. 5 ingredients for a robust multi-agent system Five design choices create a robust multi-agent system Cyber-enabled models. The first component is using multiple cyber-enabled models optimized for vulnerability discovery. 5-stage harness. Next, build a 5-stage harness that includes reconnaissance, threat modeling, hunter, validation and remediation. Zero-egress sandbox. Third, ensure the sandbox is a zero-egress microVM with no internet access, no IAM role and a start-fresh invocation. 2-layer validation. Validate by running L1 static analysis and L2 dynamic security testing inside the sandbox. Require proof of trigger before closing. Rich context. Finally, the accuracy multiplier comes from feeding the system infrastructure, application and business-specific context. This system creates a continuous loop that discovers, prioritizes, validates and remediates in a way that produces the same answer every time in a provable manner that scales to thousands of repositories. 3 agents, modeled on security roles The prioritization agent thinks like a threat intel analyst. It scours the context graph, scores proximity to your crown jewels, runs classifications and looks at business impact. The validation agent thinks like a red team operator. It maps attack paths, assesses blast radius, checks for compensating controls to provide a three-value answer: exploitable, inconclusive, or not exploitable. The remediation agent thinks like a security engineer. It patches from a proven exploit. It fixes a pattern, not a single line of code. It hits every point. It delivers a test suite in the sandbox along with the pull request. These agents work together in a shared state using durable records. Each one performs its scoped role and writes back. The context moat to power system accuracy From the CyberGym tests, context improved LLM accuracy. Generic LLM accuracy sat around 65 percent. Infrastructure context brought that up to 90 percent. Adding business context took accuracy up to 95 percent. A machine speed security system requires strong context rooted in infrastructure-level security. This exists in five pillars: Formally verify every path to determine network reachability. Leverage automated reasoning over IAM policies that mathematically prove whether a policy grants unintended access. Block by default public access to your cloud. Real-time continuous inventory of every resource and configuration change. Mathematically prove security correctness deployed at scale. So how do you trust this autonomous system? Every call goes through a four-gate authorization chain. The first gate is a policy engine with two layers: IAM scoping to guard against reaching outside the boundaries you’ve set and Cedar to enforce fine-grained tool access for what actions agents are permitted to take on which resources under what conditions. This imposes deterministic guardrails for agent actions without looping in an LLM for these authorization decisions. The second gate is input validation delivered by schema checks and account binding. The third gate is a fail-closed audit where every action is logged before execution, and nothing dispatches if the audit fails. The fourth gate is the credential broker scoped to one action, one resource with a 15-minute time to live (TTL). As mentioned earlier, the sandbox is zero-egress with no internet connectivity or service endpoints. Memory is destroyed after each task. If something goes wrong inside the sandbox, the issue remains isolated there. We layer on graduated autonomy to handle the spectrum of risk. Guardrail tolerance could look like: 80 percent autonomous for removing unused permissions 60 percent autonomous for tightening security groups 20 percent autonomy for modifying IAM roles Zero autonomy for deleting resources – only humans can take this action Finally, add three-value output transparency. Every decision cites evidence with a confidence score. LLM judgment is separated from deterministic math. Full W3C tracing with 90-day retention. These elements create a governed system for the LLM with durable records instead of chats and explicit state instead of prompts. Delivering machine-speed security Anyone can wrap a model in a harness and build a user interface. But that’s a commodity play destined for higher rates of inaccuracies and incomplete remediations. A robust system needs infrastructure context from where your workloads live, formal verification that produces traceable results, and a governed control plane. Detection is solved. Every commercial scanning tool can find security events. The hard part is building a trustworthy autonomous system that understands what a problem means in your environment and then helps move the organization toward the right response.
summary: Frontier AI advancements have created a world where exploitation outpaces defense. The average enterprise takes 32 to 43 days to patch , but the mean time to exploit a vulnerability is 10 hours . This asymmetry creates questions around how enterprises can trust autonomous AI to operate ubiquitously across their environments. As I mentioned on the TechCrunch Disrupt stage last week, security at machine speed means AI accelerates the fix as quickly as it does the find.

title: 14 ways attackers abuse cloud services to hack your enterprise
raw_text: Attackers are increasingly abusing trusted SaaS platforms, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems to blend malicious activity into legitimate enterprise traffic. Adversaries are pushing command and control (C2) through high-reputation services, including OpenAI and AWS, to blend in with normal business traffic and evade blocklists. The shift from “ living off the land ” to “living off the cloud” reflects how attackers have adapted to the enterprise’s migration of IT infrastructure to hybrid and cloud environments such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. “Instead of abusing local binaries like PowerShell or WMI [Windows Management Instrumentation] to evade detection, adversaries now leverage native cloud administrative tools, APIs, identity systems, and management consoles to operate using legitimate functionality,” says Arif Khan, head of threat hunting and response services at Mitiga. “Because cloud environments are inherently API-driven, attackers who obtain valid credentials or tokens can enumerate resources, extract data, escalate privileges, and maintain persistence through routine-looking administrative calls.” Hacking cloud-based systems bypasses traditional defenses that rely heavily on domain reputation and static blocklists. Running attack infrastructure from the cloud also makes attacks easier to mount. “Attackers are increasingly using legitimate cloud services as part of their attack infrastructure,” says Fredrik Almroth, security researcher and co-founder at Detectify. “Instead of operating their own command-and-control servers, they route traffic through trusted platforms like cloud storage, collaboration tools, or AI APIs. To defenders, it can look like routine traffic to a reputable provider.” Below are some examples of how attackers are increasingly abusing cloud-based services to mount a variety of attacks. Covert command-and-control via cloud-hosted productivity tools Researchers from Google and Mandiant recently disrupted a suspected Chinese cyber-espionage operation (UNC2814) that was abusing legitimate Google Sheets functionality to evade detection. The Gridtide malware at the center of the campaign connected to a threat actor–controlled Google spreadsheet for C2, effectively allowing it to blend in with normal network traffic. The malware treats Google Sheets as a live C2 database, using a Service Account token to poll specific cells for instructions before writing results from tasks back into adjacent columns. “This is part of an ongoing trend of actors increasingly finding success in abusing SaaS platforms as an alternative to creating and maintaining their own custom infrastructure,” according to Google’s researchers. Hiding command-and-control in trusted APIs Attackers are also forging malware that routes C2 traffic through trusted services such as OpenAI APIs. For example, the SesameOp backdoor routes traffic through OpenAI’s Assistants API , masking C2 communications as legitimate AI development work. “In cases such as the SesameOp backdoor , traffic looks like normal AI development activity,” says Parthiban Jegatheesan, managing director at Peneto Labs. “To security tools, it blends in with legitimate business use, making it much harder to block without breaking real workflows.” Malware such as VEILDrive and malign variants of the Havoc Framework post-exploitation framework abuse the Microsoft Graph API. “The malware authenticates to a legitimate corporate SharePoint or OneDrive tenant where it utilizes Graph API to read command files such as cmd.txt and write ‘output’ files (e.g., results.json) directly into a folder that looks like a user’s personal backup,” explains Kwangyun Keum, a senior offensive security engineer. Cloud service and identity abuse Attackers are targeting OAuth tokens, service accounts, and cloud APIs to move through enterprise environments while flying under the radar of conventional malware detection. In September, healthcare technology firm Veradigm admitted attackers abused a third-party vendor’s credentials to access “certain personal data of patients, including, in some instances, Social Security numbers.” The Gentlemen ransomware group claimed responsibility for the attack and threatened to publicly release stolen data. Veradigm played down the significance of the breach , stating only a small number of customers were impacted and stated neither clinical nor medical data was exposed. “The company says the credentials reached only that interface, not its wider network,” says Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “Attackers didn’t compromise server resources but rather exploited a trusted identity with a path to sensitive data. This is the epitome of ‘living off the cloud.’” Remote wipe US medical-device manufacturer Stryker suffered a destructive cyberattack in March after attackers reportedly gained access to its Microsoft Intune cloud endpoint management platform. Iran-linked hacktivist group Handala reportedly used the compromised access to wipe thousands of employee laptops and mobile devices. Stryker acknowledged the attack had affected its operations and caused global disruption . “The impact reached beyond the company: Health systems rescheduled some surgical procedures when Stryker couldn’t deliver patient-specific implants and components,” says Black Duck’s Lewis. “The cloud management plane is now the attack surface, and a compromised admin account can do what once required custom malware.” Malware staging in object storage Attackers are increasingly storing second-stage payloads or configuration files in cloud storage services — for example, S3-compatible buckets — instead of their own servers. “These files are pulled down only when needed, reducing the malware footprint on disk and allowing attackers to swap payloads without redeploying malware,” Peneto Labs’ Jegatheesan says. Data exfiltration via trusted services Attackers have also shifted from traditional FTP drops or risky pastebin (text storage) sites to exfiltrating massive troves of sensitive data via everyday cloud-based corporate communication tools such as Slack and Discord, according to Nicholas Carroll, manager cyber incident response at Nightwing. Carroll says that in recent attack campaigns threat actors “configured compromised servers to execute HTTPS POST requests to api.slack.com, hooks.slack.com, or discord.com,” using these endpoints to exfiltrate “heavily monitored secrets such as AWS Access Keys, SSH keys, and internal API tokens directly into attacker-controlled chat channels.” Hybrid and multi-stage kill chains entirely inside the cloud Several campaigns demonstrate full cloud-native attack chains, including one campaign linked to a Chinese cyberespionage group. “Since March 2024, Genesis Panda has systematically weaponized cloud services across the full attack chain — querying AWS Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) for credential harvesting, using cloud storage for payload hosting, routing C2 through domains impersonating legitimate cloud services, and using cloud compute for data exfiltration,” says Diptamay Sanyal, a principal engineer at CrowdStrike. “The cloud isn’t a target here — it’s the entire operational backbone,” Sanyal adds. Phishing and social engineering via trusted platforms Attackers are increasingly hosting lures and login pages on legitimate cloud infrastructure. For example, Russia-nexus hacking group Cozy Bear (APT 29) delivered phishing links redirecting to authentic Microsoft login pages, removing the most common phishing red flag — suspicious domains. “Victims only ever saw legitimate Microsoft infrastructure, making traditional URL-based detection useless,” says Sanyal. Trusted cloud platforms are hosting the attack infrastructure of many cybercriminals. “Phishing kits including EvilTokens , Tycoon2FA, and Kali365 rely heavily on Cloudflare’s workers.dev and similar developer platforms to host phishing pages, while AI copies a target’s branding from a single URL,” says Brandon Tirado, VP of GreyMatter Operations at threat intelligence firm ReliaQuest. “Because these services have legitimate uses, the pages tend to get past email gateways and signature detection.” Serverless and ephemeral infrastructure abuse Attackers are abusing serverless services, such as AWS Lambda or Azure Functions, to conduct network reconnaissance and scanning. The tactic was deployed during the HazyBeacon campaign targeting governmental entities in Southeast Asia and uncovered by Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 threat intel division. “Instead of scanning a target from a single compromised server, which gets its IP blocked immediately, the attacker spins up thousands of ephemeral Lambda functions,” says Kaveh Ranjbar, co-founder and CEO of Whisper Security, and ex-CIO/CTO of RIPE NCC. “Each function scans a small slice of the target network and then dies.” The traffic originates from high-reputation Amazon IPs that rotate constantly. Enterprise firewalls cannot block these IPs without breaking their own access to legitimate AWS services. “The attacker effectively ‘launders’ their traffic through Amazon’s reputation,” Ranjbar adds. Cloud tunneling Adversaries are bypassing inbound firewall rules by utilizing legitimate “tunnelling” services hosted on major cloud providers. “An attacker compromises an internal server but cannot open a port to listen for commands due to the corporate firewall,” Whisper Security’s Ranjbar explains. “So, they install a Cloudflare Tunnel or ngrok agent. This agent initiates an outbound connection to the cloud provider, which is usually allowed.” Ranjbar adds: “To the security team, this looks like legitimate, encrypted HTTPS traffic going to Cloudflare or AWS. In reality, it is a stable C2 channel that tunnels right through the perimeter defenses using trusted infrastructure as the carrier.” EBS snapshot sharing Cybercrime groups such as Scattered Spider and Storm-0501 abuse the “snapshot sharing technique,” creating a high-impact IaaS attack vector in the process. The approach bypasses traditional network security by weaponizing the cloud’s management layer. “Rather than downloading malicious files, the adversary creates a snap ‘photograph’ of the victim server’s entire hard drive and simply ‘shares’ it using the ModifySnapshotAttribute API with an external cloud account the attackers control,” says offensive security engineer Keum. “The attacker subsequently restores the snapshot and then perform attacks such as ‘offline’ credential dumping.” Trust abuse via Entra ID tenant relationships China-nexus actor Murky Panda compromised upstream IT service providers to silently pivot into downstream victims through trusted Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) tenant connections, according to CrowdStrike. Hacking into Entra ID tenant configurations to gain admin privileges is also a feature of ransomware group Storm-0501’s tradecraft . Pulling secrets directly from cloud vaults Groups such as Storm-0501 have abused cloud-native secrets stores such as AWS Secrets Manager to harvest credentials as part of its broader ransomware and extortion campaigns. “Instead of dumping credentials from endpoints, attackers query secrets directly through cloud APIs,” says Peneto Labs’ Jegatheesan. “This avoids endpoint detection and shifts the attack into places many security teams monitor less closely.” Touching the void Miscreants have even built cloud-native malware made up of custom loaders, implants, rootkits, and modular plugins, and designed to achieve persistence on compromised targets. For example, VoidLink is a highly advanced malware framework purpose-built to compromise major cloud infrastructures such as AWS, Azure, GCP, and Kubernetes clusters. The framework, apparently built and maintained by Chinese-affiliated developers, was first identified by researchers from Check Point.
summary: Attackers are increasingly abusing trusted SaaS platforms, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems to blend malicious activity into legitimate enterprise traffic. Adversaries are pushing command and control (C2) through high-reputation services, including OpenAI and AWS, to blend in with normal business traffic and evade blocklists. The shift from “ living off the land ” to “living off the cloud” reflects how attackers have adapted to the enterprise’s migration of IT infrastructure to hybrid and cloud environments such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. “Instead of abusing local binaries like PowerShell or WMI [Windows Management Instrumentation] to evade detection, adversaries now leverage native cloud administrative tools, APIs, identity systems, and management consoles to operate using legitimate functionality,” says Arif Khan, head of threat hunting and response services at Mitiga.

title: US bans DeepSeek across federal agencies, putting AI supply chains under scrutiny
raw_text: DeepSeek has been dealt a huge blow in the US, even as it continues to innovate and keep pace with, or in some cases outperform, rival models from American labs. The US Secretary of Homeland Security has issued an order banning all DeepSeek products and services from federal agencies. Government organizations must purge their IT systems of it within 60 days; those with “compelling justification” can make a case for exemption by written request to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) cited multiple concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty , lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities. Analyst Erik Avakian , technical counselor at Infotech, understands the concern. “When organizations use any type of hosted AI service, they’re potentially sending intellectual property, confidential business information, or other sensitive data into an environment where they may have very little visibility or control over what happens to it,” he said. Government concerns According to a document published in the US Federal Register , all technology developed by China-based Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. will be banned from procurement by federal civilian agencies. This includes affiliated products and any third-party tools or software built using DeepSeek implementations. Affected civilian executive branch agencies include the Departments of Treasury, State, and Justice; it does not apply, however, to private consumers, the general public, state/local governments, or Department of Defense (DoD) national security systems. “DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” the Order stated. To begin with, the company’s servers are located in the People’ s Republic of China (PRC), whose legal system grants “extensive authority” to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private infrastructure. DeepSeek’s account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users, the Order asserted. Its prompt response process may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC. This could give it “actionable intelligence” on US programs or individual users. Further, the Order stated, DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. DHS pointed to open-source security research published in February 2025 that uncovered many iOS mobile apps with multiple critical vulnerabilities. Until the ban takes full effect, DHS advised agencies to mitigate risk by monitoring inbound and outbound data traffic, implementing enhanced logging and controls on data exfiltration, and detecting and flagging anomalous activity. Agencies can submit requests for exceptions to the ban in writing, and must provide a “compelling justification,” such as its impact on mission-critical functions, or other considerations related to national interest such as national security reviews, investigations, or security agreements, as reasons why such exemption should be granted,. Security issues are rampant The ban comes just as DeepSeek is open-sourcing DeepInfer, its in-house interference framework. DeepInfer powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with what the company said is high throughput and low latency. It features high-performance kernels, an optimized inference engine, structured outputs, and speculative decoding. DeepSeek said its production token encoding and decoding components, which are aligned with processing logic behind the DeepSeek API, will bring the “same API behavior to community deployments.” “Open models. Open kernels. Open inference,” DeepSeek posted to social media site X . “From private deployments to public clouds, we’ll keep working with the community to make large-scale inference more efficient.” This isn’t its first roadblock from a cybersecurity perspective . Most notably, in January 2025, the company leaked more than one million log entries, including chat histories, API secrets, and other sensitive information, through an unsecured database. DeepSeek reportedly addressed the exposure, but it still raised questions about the overall security practices surrounding the platform, particularly for organizations considering entrusting it with their own sensitive business information, Avakian pointed out. That’s not to imply that every DeepSeek model is “inherently malicious,” he said, but there are still major questions around data privacy, the potential for information access under Chinese laws, the security of the broader AI ecosystem, and the susceptibility of DeepSeek’s models to jailbreaks and manipulation. “Taken together, [these issues] raise legitimate concerns about whether organizations can adequately understand and manage the risks involved,” Avakian said. Enterprises should seriously assess associated risk Enterprises are increasingly exploring DeepSeek, although most publicly-documented adoption has been in China, Avakian noted. Some DeepSeek models have also been made available through platforms like Microsoft Azure and AWS. “There’s genuine enterprise interest in the technology, as organizations look for opportunities to improve productivity, offer new capabilities, or reduce costs,” Avakian said. Useful applications include document summarization, internal research, and coding assistance. DeepInfer also has the potential to reduce costs, but possible benefits should be weighed against associated security risks, he pointed out. The framework was just released, so organizations are going to need to validate the claimed efficiencies in their own environments rather than assuming savings will automatically translate into lower operating costs. He encouraged organizations to start with relatively low-risk use cases, preferably using “public, synthetic, or appropriately sanitized information,” within a sandboxed environment they control themselves. The important question to ask: ‘What is the business problem we’re trying to solve?’ From there, Avakian said, determine whether DeepSeek is the best way to solve it, validate security controls, and expand the use cases based on risk tolerance. Effective governance and risk assessment are key, he noted: understand what you’re bringing into your environment, validate its security, restrict its permissions, and make sure you can monitor what it’s doing. “Approach this like any other software supply chain decision,” Avakian advised. “The fact that something is open source, inexpensive, or technically impressive doesn’t automatically make it appropriate for enterprise use.” Impact on the broader AI ecosystem The fact that the Order also addressed third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations is important, Avakian said, because organizations may be using DeepSeek technologies indirectly, through vendors, software platforms, or other services, without necessarily knowing what’s operating underneath. “These are classic supply chain issues,” he observed. It’s no longer enough to know which AI applications employees are using; enterprises must understand which models, frameworks, dependencies, and external services are embedded in products they’re purchasing and deploying, Avakian said. This means revisiting AI inventories, potentially updating procurement requirements, and expanding processes around third-party risk management, he advised. “Ultimately, enterprises leveraging these tools need to understand not only the AI technologies they’re intentionally deploying, but also the technologies they’re inheriting through third parties,” he said. This article originally appeared on CIO.com .

Government organizations must purge their IT systems of it within 60 days; those with “compelling justification” can make a case for exemption by written request to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) cited multiple concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty , lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities.

title: Enterprises should report AI breaches and ‘near misses,’ says UK financial regulator
raw_text: Enterprises should be required to report “significant AI failures and near-misses,” UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Chief Data Officer Jessica Rusu said Monday, adding to the drumbeat of demands for some kind of regulatory control over enterprise AI deployments. But her speech also highlighted regulator frustration over futile attempts to slow down the seemingly unstoppable agentic and genAI rollouts, as reports of agent misbehavior and the lack of meaningful consequences continue to emerge with alarming frequency. Rusu , speaking to a Bloomberg UK Policy Series audience, said that firms need to invest more in cyber and operational resilience. “Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognized, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too,” Rusu said . “It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress, or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.” She added, “the FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators, and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.” One of the questions that came out of the speech is what precisely was meant by “significant AI failures and near-misses.” Questions to FCA to clarify their terminology were not answered by publication time. AI failure vs near miss But Pieter Arntz , a malware intelligence researcher at security firm Malwarebytes, offered his own take on what those terms likely mean. “A significant AI failure is one with serious consequences, not simply an incorrect answer. In financial services, that could mean an AI system authorizing substantial fraudulent payments, exposing sensitive customer information, denying customers access to essential financial services, or triggering transactions that threaten market integrity,” Arntz said. “The test should be the scale and severity of the impact, rather than whether the failure looks technically dramatic.” On the other hand, he added, “An AI near-miss is an event that could realistically have caused serious harm, but was caught before that harm occurred. For example, an AI agent might attempt an unauthorized transfer that a separate approval control blocks, or a prompt-injection attack might induce it to disclose sensitive information, only for an outbound security control to stop the disclosure.” However, Arntz warned of the risk to Rusu’s approach, should the final penalties be underwhelming. “There is a risk of this becoming a paper tiger if compliance amounts to filing a report and absorbing a predictable fine,” he said. Warnings from multiple directions UK-based Gartner VP analyst Nader Henein said he is skeptical about the significance of the FCA’s proposal, in part because so many UK enterprises already have to comply with EU regulations, which have started asking companies to make such disclosures. “Financial watchdogs including the Bank of England (BoE), the UAE Central Bank, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore have all issued warnings,” he said. “A few months ago, the European central banks, together with the European Systemic Risk Board, escalated the cyber risk assessment level associated with frontier models to ‘severe,’ warning that simultaneous cyber incidents could impact the financial sector. They acknowledged that AI-driven cyber incidents now threaten core financial sector stability.” Henein said that he is especially skeptical that meaningful changes will occur in the financial sector. “Financial institutions tend to heed the warnings of the regulator that decides whether they can continue to operate, but without clear laws, regulatory oversight, and the obligatory fines, these disjointed statements are not likely to make a difference,” he said. Could ‘incentivize the wrong behavior’ Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, added that one risk of this increased visibility requirement is that it could inadvertently incentivize the wrong behavior. “A bank with good monitoring may catch hundreds of attempts by AI agents to act outside their authority,” he said. “A bank with poor monitoring may report zero, because it never saw them. On paper, the safer bank looks worse. A model failing a red-team test is the test working, not a regulatory incident.” However, Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, said that the near-miss approach has the strongest potential to change the conversation. “I love the near-miss idea. It is the most important thing in the speech. It is the part financial firms are least ready for,” he said. But, he stressed, “[Rusu] also warns about reliance on a single model. An outage at one AI supplier that takes down a customer service channel counts, too.” Another concern about reliance on a specific model is the ever-present risk that an AI vendor could change the model without telling all of its customers. “A model can pass testing in March and misbehave in May without anyone at the firm changing a line of code, because the provider changed the model underneath,” Dickson said. “A model version change should get the same scrutiny as any other production change.” This article originally appeared on CIO.com .
