But her speech also highlighted regulator frustration over futile attempts to slow down the seemingly unstoppable agentic and genAI rollouts, as reports of agent misbehavior and the lack of meaningful consequences continue to emerge with alarming frequency. Rusu , speaking to a Bloomberg UK Policy Series audience, said that firms need to invest more in cyber and operational resilience. “Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses.

title: KVM escape exposes broader attack surface in Linux networking
raw_text: Security researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s networking stack that can let attackers escape a KVM virtual machine and execute code on the host system. The weakness could also potentially let attackers compromise systems running other Linux-based virtualization and sandbox platforms. Tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and dubbed PwnEscape , the vulnerability was discovered by researchers from AI-powered pentesting startup Pwn.ai during a $1 million challenge to hack Vercel’s sandbox platform , which uses KVM-based Firecracker microVMs. Rather than exploiting a bug in the KVM hypervisor itself, the attack targets the Linux networking code that handles traffic from inside virtual machines. Specially crafted packets can alter an IPv4 header after the host’s kernel has already validated it, causing later processing to trust packet data that attackers have manipulated. The Pwn.ai researchers demonstrated host-memory leakage against Vercel’s production sandboxes and separately achieved host crashes and root-level code execution on researcher-controlled systems. Vercel confirmed the findings but said no reports showed access to customer files, secrets, or application data. A fix was merged into the mainline Linux kernel with patched kernel versions now available for multiple distributions. Administrators need to deploy those kernel updates on host systems because updating only guest VMs does not fix the vulnerability. Checksum processing rewrites validated headers The flaw involves checksum offloading, a performance optimization that allows Linux to postpone calculating a packet’s checksum. Alongside the packet, the kernel carries metadata specifying where that calculation should begin and where its result should be written, but in virtual networking those instructions can originate from an untrusted guest. The vulnerable implementation failed to ensure that completing the checksum would leave the already-validated IPv4 header untouched, meaning that guest-controlled metadata could directly write into that header, changing the advertised length before the packet was split into smaller fragments for transmission. In their demonstration, the researchers managed to change the header length from 20 to 60 bytes, while the packet buffer held only 28 bytes of valid data. The fragmentation process then copied 32 bytes beyond that valid data into outgoing packets, leaking host memory. By repeating the process, the researchers were able to make observations and control memory allocations to achieve host-kernel memory writes to run a helper program as root. The complete exploitation steps that take this attack from a memory leak to code execution have not been publicly revealed yet, but the researchers plan a separate write-up. “The allocator-sensitive write chain, object-lifetime controls, and other hypervisor-specific adaptation are large enough to require a separate article,” they said. “Although we suspect the security industry will use this post to figure out the other affected hypervisors and we expect exploits in weaker configurations to arrive in weeks, and exploits working in default hypervisor configurations to arrive in under a month.” The attack surface extends beyond KVM PwnEscape differs from other VM escape attacks that target the hypervisor’s handling of virtual CPUs or memory. The Januscape vulnerability disclosed earlier this year , for example, affected KVM’s memory-management code, but with this exploit the vulnerable code is in the Linux host’s IPv4 networking subsystem. The researchers warn that similar bugs could exist elsewhere in the networking stack, wherever guest-controlled metadata can modify packet fields after those fields have already passed validation. The accepted patch , authored by Red Hat developer Michael S. Tsirkin, adds validation at five checksum completion points, including IPv4 fragmentation, bridge connection tracking, and packet filtering, but the patch commit message states that “a more complete validation at input is forthcoming, but needs more work.” The flaw’s impact for other hypervisors and container technologies remains to be seen. Red Hat lists OpenShift Container Platform components as affected , but other virtualization technologies like Docker or Xen have not issued advisories yet. The guest-to-host attack requires an attacker-controlled workload capable of supplying the malformed traffic through the virtual network. As a result, admins of environments that allow the execution of untrusted code inside VMs need to take action as soon as possible. “A VM escape is another kernel vulnerability because KVM lives inside the Linux kernel, but it has more serious implications,” Alex Zenla, CTO and co-founder of container security firm Edera, told CSO. “When a guest breaks out, it isn’t escaping into some neatly contained hypervisor; it can land in the lowest levels of the operating system that owns the host’s processes, drivers, and network stack. This is critical and a very different security proposition from a hypervisor designed with a deliberately tiny privileged layer.” KVM and other kernel-based virtualization components have had multiple critical vulnerabilities this year, some of them found with the help of LLMs, including PwnEscape. Meanwhile AI agents have been observed attempting to break out of sandboxes during tests. This challenges the workload isolation assumptions in virtualized environments. “Security architecture has to assume that eventually, something will be compromised and make sure that compromise doesn’t become total host ownership,” Zenla said. AWS says its managed EC2, Lambda, and Fargate services are unaffected by CVE-2026-99999, but customers running their own KVM virtual machines with virtio-net networking on vulnerable hosts need to apply the relevant kernel updates. Administrators should follow their distribution’s advisories because the fixes can be backported to older kernel versions.
summary: Security researchers have found a critical flaw in the Linux kernel’s networking stack that can let attackers escape a KVM virtual machine and execute code on the host system. The weakness could also potentially let attackers compromise systems running other Linux-based virtualization and sandbox platforms. Tracked as CVE-2026-99999 and dubbed PwnEscape , the vulnerability was discovered by researchers from AI-powered pentesting startup Pwn.ai during a $1 million challenge to hack Vercel’s sandbox platform , which uses KVM-based Firecracker microVMs. Rather than exploiting a bug in the KVM hypervisor itself, the attack targets the Linux networking code that handles traffic from inside virtual machines.

title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs and employ more artificial intelligence
raw_text:
Barclays Bank is planning to reduce its headcount by 5,000 as technology such as artificial intelligence (AI) drives cost-cutting.

The number equates to 5% of the bank’s total workforce and adds to the AI-fuelled cuts seen at major banks this year.

The UK bank said 60% of the cuts will come from support functions, including the need for “fewer developers as AI makes our people more productive”.

Speaking at a results meeting, the bank’s CEO, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the job cuts were the result of technology investments.

“AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” he said. “I’ve often said that it is the icing on the cake – it’s not the cake – because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI.”

Barclays Bank said it expects to make efficiency savings of £1.1bn in 2027, with the actions taken expected to reduce “5,000 full-time employees”.

A spokesperson at the high street bank said: “We are positioning Barclays for the future, building the workforce and skills needed to deliver our strategy and meet the evolving needs of our customers and clients. In doing so, we are committed to helping our colleagues develop and build rewarding careers, while meeting the changing needs of customers and clients and ensuring Barclays continues to succeed in the years ahead.”

Earlier this month, HSBC announced plans to cut half of its management and specialist positions in wealth management and reduce the number of human financial advisers by 70%. The bank is using AI to replace them through cuts described as “deep, wide and brutal”.

Furthermore, HSBC investment bank boss Michael Roberts recently said AI agents could replace humans trading in financial markets in a few years, due to the combination of advances in AI, quantum computing and distributed ledger technology.

In an interview with Bloomberg TV, Roberts stressed that humans need to remain “in the loop”, adding: “I think quantum computing will be able to look at very complex types of market movements, and with the advent of AI – which will make that even quicker – you can see agents trading bonds using quantum computing. That’s the future.”

Separately, and in a different industry, the boss of Indian IT services giant Infosys dismissed fears of AI taking jobs as “hogwash”, stating that the technology will fuel demand for new human skills.

Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi, Infosys chairman Nandan Nilekani stressed the need for people to provide the skills needed for AI to deliver.

“Business transformation is not just about coding – 70% is governance, change management, transformation, guardrails,” he said.

Nilekani asked: “How do you make sure AI bots don’t hallucinate? How do you make sure agents don’t go rogue?”

Answering his own question, he said the need for people was “more than ever before” for companies like Infosys.

  • Survey shows that half of UK banks will increase spending on artificial intelligence as more see AI-related productivity gains.
  • AI-related roles could be the only “safe jobs” in the banking sector as financial organisations ‘relentlessly’ press on with AI-led transformation.

title: Interview: IQT, the organisation with roots in the CIA
raw_text:
IQT is an unusual beast, in that it is a technology company investor, but one that operates in a way that is a far stretch from the private equity concerns and venture capitalists that reside on Sand Hill Road and put their billions of dollars behind Silicon Valley startups and scaleups.

Instead, IQT is a not-for-profit that funds companies with technologies it believes can support the national security interests of the US and allies. Headquartered in Virginia, it also works across offices in London, Munich, Sydney and Singapore.

Set up in 1999 by the CIA, the organisation says it has made more than 850 investments in its 27-year history, with over 50 of those companies now valued at over $1bn. Readers may recognise some familiar names from that portfolio, including data discovery firm Databricks and DevSecOps software engineering platform GitLab. Others are about as “deep tech” as it is possible to go, spanning semiconductor, space, biotechnology and artificial intelligence (AI) specialists.

We put some questions to the organisation’s executive vice-president, international, Jennifer Nelson, who is responsible for non-US investment activities and growing IQT’s global operations – it has invested in over 20 overseas organisations. Nelson is a 15-year veteran of IQT, with roles including chief of staff, managing programmes in security acquisitions and aligning with the CIA. She previously worked at IBM in public sector technology strategy setting.

You make investments to secure the US and its allies. With the recent shifts in geopolitics and US-international relationships, has your roster of specified allies also changed?

No, our mission and roster of allies haven’t changed. IQT was created to serve US national security, and we’ve long worked alongside our allies, including the UK and Australian governments. What has changed is the innovation landscape itself. Important technologies now emerge from a wider range of countries, each with distinct strengths based on their research institutions, industrial capacity and strategic priorities. IQT continues to focus on trusted partners and allied ecosystems – that hasn’t changed – but the need to understand global innovation has grown.

For IQT, the priority is consistent – ensuring government partners have access to the most relevant technologies, wherever they develop, and the value of strong relationships with trusted partners and allied innovation ecosystems continues to grow.

The US government has said it may take equity stakes in AI companies. Is that the plan?

Governments around the world are reevaluating how best to engage with technologies that are becoming strategically important for economic competitiveness and national security. The US is no exception. Discussions about equity stakes in AI companies are part of that broader exploration, but the mechanisms may vary.

What is clear is that AI is now a foundational technology with implications that extend far beyond any one sector. The larger question, and the one I think matters most, is how governments ensure they can understand, adopt and benefit from these rapidly evolving technologies. IQT’s model already addresses part of this challenge by helping translate commercial innovation into responsible, operationally meaningful capability.

“The future will not be shaped by a single breakthrough technology, but by multiple technologies working together in ways that create entirely new capabilities”

Jennifer Nelson, IQT

What new and emerging technologies do you see as being potential sources for your investment portfolio?

We’re seeing strong momentum in cyber security, advanced manufacturing, energy systems, quantum technologies, maritime innovation, and a range of dual-use capabilities. Many of the most interesting opportunities come from the convergence of domains – AI with quantum, autonomy with edge compute, new materials with resilient energy storage. The future will not be shaped by a single breakthrough technology, but by multiple technologies working together in ways that create entirely new capabilities.

Across all of these areas, the focus is on operational resilience. Government customers increasingly need technologies that can function in contested or resource‑constrained environments, not just perform well in a clean lab setting.

And, same question as above, but with reference to blue-sky tech?

Blue-sky technologies often emerge from intersections of fields. We’re watching advances in autonomous systems across land, sea, air and space; breakthroughs in materials science; next-generation energy approaches; and quantum systems that could reshape computation or sensing.

The common thread is that these aren’t incremental improvements. They have the potential to meaningfully change what is possible, and those shifts often have long-term implications for national security.

The technologies you invest in are, obviously, areas with high-premium valuations, and we have seen eye-popping valuations for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. Is that changing the cost/economics model and the way you invest?

AI valuations have certainly been headline-grabbing, but they haven’t changed IQT’s core model. Our primary objective is to identify and deliver government partners access to strategically important technologies. That means we evaluate companies based on relevance, resilience and whether their capabilities can actually be adopted by national security customers, not on valuation trends.

From my perspective, what has changed is the pace and the stakes. AI is now a foundational technology, and understanding how it can be deployed – with the right governance and mission alignment – has become even more important. In many cases, the real value IQT brings is helping companies translate powerful technology into something that works in complex, real-world environments.

As a non-profit, what pressures, if any, do you have to show some sort of financial or non-financial return on investment or ability to hit key performance indicators (KPIs)?

IQT evaluates success through mission impact, not financial returns. Our KPIs are tied to the ability to move strategically important technologies into government use. That includes identifying capabilities with clear mission relevance, helping founders understand national security needs, and ensuring technologies can be deployed securely, reliably and at scale.

This model has worked for more than 25 years because it stays focused on the operational outcome.

Could your status as a non-profit change?

Our non-profit structure is a key part of what allows IQT to operate effectively at the intersection of government, startups and the broader innovation ecosystem. It gives us independence, helps us build trusted relationships across sectors, and keeps the mission at the centre of every decision. In theory, structures can change, but there is no focus on doing so.

Are there any areas of technology that you would not deem suitable for investment for any reason?

We don’t exclude broad categories of technology. The primary filter is mission alignment: does the capability address a meaningful challenge for government stakeholders and can it deliver resilient, real-world impact? We evaluate each opportunity on that basis.

Maritime technology is receiving increasing attention. Why is maritime innovation so important to national security?

The maritime domain underpins much of the global economy and a significant portion of the world’s critical infrastructure. Undersea cables carry the majority of international data traffic, and keeping global trade moving depends on secure shipping routes. Both play a role in national resilience. At the same time, advances in autonomous systems, sensors and artificial intelligence are creating entirely new possibilities for maritime awareness and operations.

We’ve seen this in our portfolio. For example, Sofar Ocean, an IQT portfolio company, operates one of the world’s largest privately owned ocean sensor networks, deploying solar-powered Spotter buoys that generate more than 1.5 million real-time observations across the globe. The data is leveraged by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the US Navy to support weather forecasting, navigation and maritime domain awareness.

As geopolitical competition intensifies, maritime innovation is becoming central to protecting these vital environments.

How many of your investments are non-US headquartered companies?

Whilst IQT remains a champion of US innovation, it has investments in more than 20 countries, and approximately 15% of our portfolio is based outside the US. That reflects a simple reality – strategically important technologies can originate anywhere, and engaging with global ecosystems strengthens the capabilities available to the US and its allies.

How do your relationships with those non-US-based organisations differ from those you have with US firms?

The underlying objective is the same – accelerate groundbreaking technologies that strengthen national security for America and its allies. What differs is the context. Companies in different regions often respond to unique industrial strengths, regulatory environments and local security needs. Understanding those contexts helps us tailor how we evaluate and support them.

What is the typical profile of an organisation you will invest in?

We look for companies developing game-changing technologies with potential relevance to government or national security challenges. Strong technical differentiation, a leadership team capable of executing, and credible pathways to scale are important factors. Unlike traditional venture firms, we evaluate every investment through two lenses: commercial viability and mission impact. A company doesn’t need to be building for government today. Many of our most successful investments began as purely commercial products that we helped adapt for national security use cases.

IQT’s model combines three steps: identifying the technology; evaluating how it can best serve the current and future needs of our government partners; and helping adapt it for operational deployment. Doing so by drawing on more than 25 years of experience bridging the startup ecosystem and the national security community. That approach isn’t limited to the United States. Through our international offices, we apply the same model in support of allied nations as well.”

Do you ever take majority stakes?

No, IQT does not seek control positions. Our role is to support companies developing strategically important capabilities, not to direct their operations. We focus on helping them grow, mature and navigate pathways into government adoption where appropriate.

How important are universities and research institutions in helping turn early-stage technologies into scalable, deployable capabilities?

Universities and research institutions are essential to early-stage innovation, especially in areas like AI, quantum technologies, biotechnology, advanced engineering and materials science. Many foundational breakthroughs originate there. The challenge is translation – turning research into deployable capabilities – and that requires collaboration between researchers, entrepreneurs, investors and end users. IQT plays a key role in that transition, helping early-stage startups with promising technologies mature into companies that can operate reliably in demanding environments. 

One recent example from our portfolio is Diraq, which is building quantum computers based on modified silicon transistors. Based in Sydney, Australia, with a growing presence in the US, Diraq spun out of the University of New South Wales, where years of research funding, facilities and hardware support laid the groundwork for its commercialisation in quantum computing – a field that remains very research-centric.

IQT engaged with Diraq through its early commercialisation and invested in October 2025. Diraq was recently one of nine companies – and the only international company – selected for the latest instalment of Chips Act funding for quantum technology. 

Do you work closely with intelligence and security agencies of other countries, such as the UK?

Yes. Innovation is global, and the security challenges we face are shared with our closest allies, making international collaboration core to IQT’s model. We work closely with the UK’s national security community and maintain a physical presence in London, which strengthens our ability to identify promising technologies emerging across the UK and Europe. We similarly maintain an office in Sydney and work closely with the Australian government. In both cases, the goal is the same: finding and supporting the startups which are building technologies that matter to allied national security missions.

Do you see your organisation as analogous to any other international organisations, or is it essentially unique?

Many organisations have sought to replicate aspects of the IQT model over the years, which we view as a positive reflection of its success. However, IQT occupies a relatively unique position at the intersection of government, venture investing and innovation. Our role isn’t simply to invest in promising companies – it’s to connect emerging technologies directly to government needs, which is a distinctive combination of mission, structure and operating approach.

What do you see as your past or current successes?

IQT’s greatest success is its consistency. For more than 25 years, we’ve helped government partners access commercially developed technologies that meaningfully strengthen national security. Today, capabilities developed by IQT-backed companies support everything from autonomous systems and data analytics to resilient communications and satellite imagery. That operational impact is our measure of success.

Are there areas you could specify where IQT performance has been sub-optimal?

Candidly, not every investment works out – that’s inherent to early-stage venture, and we’re no exception. Some technologies we backed didn’t mature on the timeline we hoped, and some markets developed differently than we anticipated. We’ve also historically been slower than we’d like to communicate our role publicly, which meant government partners and the startup community didn’t always understand how to work with us. What we try to do well is learn – our model has evolved considerably as technology cycles have compressed, and that process continues today.

What is the near-term and long-term future for IQT?

The pace of technological change shows no signs of slowing, which means the challenge of connecting innovation with operational needs will only become more important. In the near term, we expect significant advances in AI, autonomy, space, quantum technologies, manufacturing and energy systems – all areas increasingly tied to mission resilience.

Longer term, the challenge for governments will be building the capacity to continuously absorb new technologies. IQT’s role will continue to be helping partners navigate rapid change and access the innovations that matter most.

One increasingly important question is how governments build systems to adopt technology continuously, rather than treat it as a series of one-off acquisitions. Much of today’s discussion focuses on individual technologies, but long-term advantage comes from sustained integration and adaptation. That requires a durable pipeline between the startup ecosystem and government missions that surfaces new capabilities year after year, not just when a crisis demands it. IQT’s mission is to help make that possible.

title: Grid ‘runs on coal-age data’, warns Open Climate Fix
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) forecasting non-profit organisation Open Climate Fix (OCF) has published an open letter calling on ministers to unlock energy datasets, and warned that Britain’s grid is “running on data infrastructure built for the age of coal”.

The letter, published on 22 October, was backed by a coalition that includes Claire Young MP, a member of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, the Centre for Public Data, energy think tanks Ember and Regen, and a Google DeepMind researcher that signed in a personal capacity.

It argued that much of the data artificial intelligence (AI) tools need to cut bills and make the grid resilient sits with network operators, generators and suppliers, but are often locked behind private systems or published in formats that cannot easily be used. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has named access to data as the first of six barriers to AI adoption in its vision for an AI-enabled clean energy system. 

OCF sets out three demands:

  • Government should make unlocking priority energy data an explicit part of the clean power mission, using the forthcoming AI for Clean Energy Strategy as the vehicle.
  • DESNZ should expedite publication of priority datasets – network, consumption, rooftop solar, weather, flexibility and industrial energy use data – at a granularity that makes them genuinely usable.
  • Ofgem should regulate for usability, not just publication, so datasets are timely, machine-readable and standardised.

The letter pointed to rooftop solar as the clearest gap. Solar provided about 6.5% of UK electricity in 2025, but there is no public record of its live, half-hourly output. OCF – whose open source models it said have halved forecasting errors at the National Energy System Operator (NESO) – said national figures are instead estimated from data covering less than 0.3% of live solar capacity, scaled up more than 300x, at an error rate of about 5%. 

It estimated that closing the gap would quadruple the savings from its NESO partnership from £30m to £120 m a year, rising to hundreds of millions of pounds as the UK moves toward its 2035 solar targets.

“Opening up energy data is one of the few solutions that needs no new power stations or cables. The forthcoming AI for Clean Energy strategy is the moment to do it,” said Dan Travers, chief executive of Open Climate Fix.

  • Burnham ministry shifts look far from fixing datacentre gridlock. Clogged grid queues and speculative planning applications threaten the UK’s 2030 datacentre and clean energy targets. Is a national ‘superministry’ the only way out?
  • Datacentre dive: AI factory power draw changes the grid calculus: We look at how the power and cooling needs of AI factories reshape grid planning.

Claire Young MP said energy bills are “rightly at the top of the government’s agenda”, and that “better grid data could be part of the answer” to bringing them down.

The letter lands as government, regulator and networks are already moving on data. Government and Ofgem’s Energy Digitalisation Framework sets a direction for coordination, but the letter argues “coordination alone will not fix this”.

Ofgem published its “Securing Open Data in Energy” consultation in May, and network operators maintain they already share “unprecedented” volumes of data. The reality is fragmented: the six distribution network operators (DNOs) publish open data on different platforms, under different licences and in different formats, so availability does not equal usability (see box below).

This all matters because AI workloads and the datacentre pipeline are among the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand, while the connection queue gets filled with speculative projects. Meanwhile, the price of an opaque grid is met in balancing charges based on gas prices that reach business and household bills.

How open is UK grid data?

A Computer Weekly scan of the six distribution network operators (DNOs) found 690 published datasets, but the data is published in ways that cannot easily be compared across regions:

  • Three different portal platforms across the six operators, meaning there is no single way to query the grid.
  • 12 different licences, including several DNO-specific terms, and 95 datasets with no licence stated at all.
  • Capacity and headroom appear under roughly 10 different names. The one standardised dataset – the Embedded Capacity Register, agreed through ENA’s Open Networks project – is still split differently by each operator.
  • Connection queues are published by only some DNOs, in incompatible formats.
  • Demand data is the most uneven: UK Power Networks publishes 15 datasets, SSEN none.

The result is that the same information cannot be pulled together without manual work – exactly the friction the letter asks Ofgem to remove.
summary:
Artificial intelligence (AI) forecasting non-profit organisation Open Climate Fix (OCF) has published an open letter calling on ministers to unlock energy datasets, and warned that Britain’s grid is “running on data infrastructure built for the age of coal”.

The letter, published on 22 October, was backed by a coalition that includes Claire Young MP, a member of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, the Centre for Public Data, energy think tanks Ember and Regen, and a Google DeepMind researcher that signed in a personal capacity.

It argued that much of the data artificial intelligence (AI) tools need to cut bills and make the grid resilient sits with network operators, generators and suppliers, but are often locked behind private systems or published in formats that cannot easily be used. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has named access to data as the first of six barriers to AI adoption in its vision for an AI-enabled clean energy system. 

OCF sets out three demands:

  • Government should make unlocking priority energy data an explicit part of the clean power mission, using the forthcoming AI for Clean Energy Strategy as the vehicle.
  • DESNZ should expedite publication of priority datasets – network, consumption, rooftop solar, weather, flexibility and industrial energy use data – at a granularity that makes them genuinely usable.
  • Ofgem should regulate for usability, not just publication, so datasets are timely, machine-readable and standardised.

The letter pointed to rooftop solar as the clearest gap. Solar provided about 6.5% of UK electricity in 2025, but there is no public record of its live, half-hourly output. OCF – whose open source models it said have halved forecasting errors at the National Energy System Operator (NESO) – said national figures are instead estimated from data covering less than 0.3% of live solar capacity, scaled up more than 300x, at an error rate of about 5%. 

It estimated that closing the gap would quadruple the savings from its NESO partnership from £30m to £120 m a year, rising to hundreds of millions of pounds as the UK moves toward its 2035 solar targets.

title: What to do as critical PHP flaws puts millions of websites at risk
raw_text:
Two critical vulnerabilities in PHP – the server-side language behind much of the public web – allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) on affected servers. Emergency patches landed on Wednesday 21 October, but they cover only PHP 8.2 and newer, leaving a long tail of older sites exposed.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) described a vulnerability that would allow an attacker to trigger an out-of-memory condition that corrupts memory and, under certain conditions, achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. In other words, the attacker gets a shell on the server and a direct path to the file system and the database.

PHP is a free, open-source, server-side scripting language created in 1994. It runs on the web server, not in the browser, to assemble page content, talk to databases and run backend logic before delivering finished HTML to a user. It sits beneath the content-management and e-commerce systems most organisations rely on, which is why the blast radius is so wide.

What to do now

  • Identify every system running PHP, prioritising internet-facing systems. Do not limit discovery to outdated versions – all versions may be affected.

  • Update to the latest fixed version of PHP (8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 or 8.5.12) and monitor for further updates.

  • For PHP 8.1 or older, contact your distribution or long-term support vendor for a backported fix, or upgrade to a supported version.

  • If you cannot patch, apply the PHP Team's temporary mitigations, or take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.

  • Before upgrading an unpatched system, check for evidence of compromise and backdoors.

The two flaws – CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 – each carry a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10 and affect every release dating back to PHP 5 in 2004. PHP powers roughly 24 million websites, according to BuiltWith, and about three-quarters of all sites whose language can be identified, according to W3Techs.

The vulnerabilities went undetected for more than a decade and were found using artificial intelligence (AI). Security firms Wiz and Calif used OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Google's Gemini 4 Argon to locate and verify them, coordinating with the PHP team before disclosure.

Official bodies around the world told organisations to act immediately. "Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the UK’s NCSC said.

The US National Security Agency (NSA) warned: "These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database. If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organisations take the system offline."

The EU's CERT-EU offered similar advice, telling operators to "consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix can be applied" where remediation could not happen at once.

Companies and organisations affected

  • Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and the WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento, phpBB, MediaWiki, Laravel, Symfony and WHMCS ecosystems

  • UK: Edinburgh Council and several BBC programme pages, including Doctor Who and The Traitors

  • Finland: government public web services (Valtori)

  • Netherlands: NCSC-NL, the Port of Rotterdam, Overheid.nl, the KNVB, several hospitals and the Tweede Kamer

  • France: Interior Ministry websites

  • Denmark: Kombit, including the national school communication platform

  • Japan: Sakura Internet suspended a database appliance function

  • DeviantArt and other consumer sites reported downtime

The impact was immediate and global. Finland's state IT provider Valtori took government public services offline "as a precautionary measure". In the Netherlands, the National Cyber Security Centre pulled its own site, alongside the Port of Rotterdam, the Overheid.nl portal, the KNVB football association and several hospitals. France's Interior Ministry placed all its sites into preventive maintenance, Denmark's Kombit shut down several services, and in the UK, Edinburgh Council and several BBC programme pages went dark.

Wikipedia, operated by the Wikimedia Foundation, said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be patched.

On Reddit's r/PHP and r/technology forums, practitioners flagged the practical realities of the fix. Administrators running older PHP 7.x sites – a large share of the WordPress estate – reported waiting on backported fixes from Linux distributions, while others noted cloud platforms such as AWS Elastic Beanstalk had yet to ship the update. Several argued the long tail of unmanaged sites would take months to patch.

Timeline

  • Early August 2026 – a security researcher first flags the issue

  • Friday 16 October – the White House says it was first made aware of the flaw

  • 20 October – PHP maintainers publish an advisory for two 9.2-severity vulnerabilities, with patches scheduled about 12 hours later

  • 20–21 October – purported exploit details and a "PHP2Shell" video leak, showing remote code execution on WordPress, MediaWiki, phpBB, Magento, Joomla, Laravel, Symfony, Drupal and WHMCS

  • Wednesday 21 October, 13:34 UTC – source fixes land in the php-src GitHub repository and patches begin rolling out

  • Wednesday 21 October – NCSC, NSA, CERT-EU and agencies in Australia and Japan urge patching or takedowns; Finland, the Netherlands, France and Denmark take sites offline

  • Commvault users told to patch two RCE exploit chains: We examine a pair of remote code execution flaws that could be used to target on-prem customers with ransomware.

title: Burnham ministry shifts look far from fixing datacentre gridlock
raw_text:
Westminster has spent a decade devolving economic decision-making away from London – to local mayors like Greater Manchester’s Andy Burnham, who, now as prime minister, wants to distribute that power across the nation.

Burnham has set out his stall. In September, he told the Commons he would not back a moratorium on new datacentres, insisting instead that communities should feel their benefits.

But championing datacentres is not the same as delivering datacentres. Grid connection queues, the price of electricity, planning portals clogged with applications that may never be built – all of these are national levers, and no amount of regional enthusiasm moves them. That’s the friction at the heart of the UK’s infrastructure problem, where regional ambition runs into a national system that’s stuck.

Two 2030 deadlines compound the urgency. These are the government’s target of 6GW of AI-capable datacentre capacity – which currently looks out of reach – and its pledge of a clean power grid. 

In this article we look at how speculative applications and grid logjams are breaking planning, why the datacentre boom and the climate target now depend on the same clogged queue, and whether centralised reform – maybe even a “superministry” for critical infrastructure – is the only way out.

Mayoral playbook vs local reality

Greater Manchester’s devolution rests on a simple proposition. Namely, that local decisions are best made locally. Across Burnham’s mayoralty, from 2017 until he entered Number 10 this year, that meant transport, housing and skills. A fourth prize has since joined them – digital infrastructure. He courted it directly. As mayor, he visited the site of Kao Data’s £350m, 40MW datacentre in Stockport, and folded it into Greater Manchester’s digital blueprint and the region’s pitch as an AI hub.

That ambition makes sense. Mayoral authorities are well versed in steering investment, tying it to local skills and jobs, and giving the region one voice. For the things devolution was built for – co-ordination, convening, local economic strategy – the logic is sound.

But a huge datacentre is not a Bee Network tramline. It needs land, water and power at a scale far beyond what a mayor can control. A mayor can champion a site, but cannot deliver a grid connection, set the industrial electricity price a developer pays, or clear a queue backlogged with speculative bids. The true deciders of these levers are in Whitehall, and with the regulator, Ofgem – not Number 10 North.

That is the structural limit of the mayoral playbook. TechUK, a London-based non-profit organisation, reaches the same diagnosis. That is, the real determinants of datacentre investment are electricity prices and reliable grid connection timelines, which are national problems, not regional. Devolution can capture the benefits but it can’t remove the blocks on its own.

Burnham now sits on both sides of that line. Bill McCluggage, a former Cabinet Office director of IT strategy, said a Burnham government “must reconcile localism with national priorities by accepting that datacentres are now critical national infrastructure”.

The speculative planning trap

The deeper issue isn’t the number of datacentres being proposed – it’s that it’s hard to tell which ones are real. Planning applications and grid requests can be speculative, lodged to hold a position rather than to break ground. That leaves local authorities, water companies and energy providers trying to forecast with no way to tell which numbers are genuine.

This uncertainty does real damage. These speculative schemes distort the national picture and make it harder for genuine operators to win a connection, but they also carry a reputational cost. As Katie Davies, head of energy and infrastructure policy at TechUK, said, speculative applications “have branded the sector with a reputation for unreasonable demand”.

Ofgem’s answer is to make holding a place costly. The regulator has warned that “speculative schemes taking up space can delay viable projects and create uncertainty for network planning”, and has proposed an upfront fee to claim a queue position.

TechUK backs the principle. Davies argued developers should “hit real milestones, such as demonstrating financial capability, to keep their place in the queue”, but parts company with the regulator on price. She warned that “Ofgem’s proposed fee of up to £712,500 per megawatt is set too high”. It would deter speculators, she said, but would “alienate genuine investors”.

Instead, TechUK proposes three measures: a proportionate fee, a financial capability requirement, and a “look-back test” that penalises speculative behaviour with temporary bans on applications. Together, said Davies, they would “do the job without pushing investment overseas”. The principle is simple: raise the cost of holding a place you never mean to use.

The grid and water visibility crisis

It’s the speculation that can bring the most expensive damage. For TechUK, the crowded grid queue is the most pressing threat to investment, with energy prices the deeper, structural problem. Davies was blunt about the scale. “Some developers are facing waits of up to 10 years for a grid connection, which threatens project financing and renders some schemes impossible to invest in,” she said.

Speculative requests sit in the queue with real projects, inflating the load the grid is told to plan for. Forecasts are built around demand that may never materialise, while real schemes wait behind applications that will never be built. Clear the speculation, and the real queue would be far shorter than the headline figures suggest.

Water faces the same problem, if less publicly. Companies in this industry can’t size investment in supply when they can’t separate genuine schemes from speculative ones, so planned upgrades risk falling behind schedule or stalling.

This is where the climate goal part of the problem bites. The National Energy System Operator has said Britain can build a clean power system by 2030 even if datacentre demand quadruples, but only if regional networks expand four times faster than in the past decade and connection delays are cleared. The climate target and the datacentre boom depend on the same clogged queue.

Whether it’s electricity or water, the common thread is information – the planning system is being asked to commit real capital against numbers it has every reason to distrust.

National governance and the superministry debate

The question is who in Whitehall owns this problem. As it stands, nobody does – and that has become even less clear. 

In July 2026, Burnham abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and scattered its remit. Here’s what happened to it:

  • AI strategy – the Cabinet Office
  • DSIT digital functions – Department for Culture, Media and Sport
  • Energy and the grid – the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ)
  • Responsibility for water – Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs
  • Planning – local government.
  • Connection decisions – Ofgem and the system operator. 
  • Clean power target and connections reform – DESNZ; the closest thing to a single owner, but it controls neither planning nor water.

A single datacentre touches all of them, yet no single department can see the whole picture. That fragmentation is the strongest case for a dedicated “superministry for critical infrastructure”. 

Such a department could set a national view for demand, grid alignment and planning timelines, as well as halt speculative applications being judged in isolation by other departments that currently only see part of the picture. 

There is an irony here: Burnham’s first reshuffle split responsibility further instead of pulling it together.

But a reshuffle alone won’t fix it. Planning is already moving, with datacentres falling under the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects regime. This provides the basis for decisions on development consent orders that replace local planning authority permissions for major infrastructure.

However, TechUK’s Davies said reform only goes so far. “This alone will not unlock investment,” she explained. “The real challenge is addressing electricity prices and providing quicker and more reliable grid connection dates.”

This is where the bigger cliff edge sits. The UK has the highest industrial electricity prices among International Energy Agency member nations. Davies noted that “a 100MW datacentre in the UK pays four times as much as an equivalent project in the US”. 

This is increasingly due to levies that fund environmental and social schemes, plus the UK's marginal-pricing structure that means gas sets the wholesale price for all electricity. 

Davies’s solution is to shift the levies into general taxation, as the government has already done in part for households.

The bottleneck is national

Devolution, Burnham-style, can help govern the upside of a datacentre boom, such as local skills and economic capture for the overall environment. The mayoral model is an advance on what came before, but the bottleneck isn’t local. Grid transparency, energy costs and the tide of speculative applications are national problems, and they can’t be solved one city-region at a time.

Whether the answer is a formal superministry or coordinated national reform matters less than whether the fixes land. These include clearing the queue of speculative place-sitters and bringing industrial power costs back to within sight of competitors.

Do that, and regional ambition has something solid to build on. Fail, and the UK risks walking into systemic infrastructure gridlock by 2030, with digital demand and climate commitments both pulling against a system that can’t tell what’s real.

title: Five resellers won one in seven UK public sector IT deals in 2025-26
raw_text:
UK public sector bodies awarded 7,994 IT contracts in the year to August 2026, worth a combined £91bn, in a market that leans heavily towards five resellers. Softcat, Phoenix Software, Insight Direct, Civica and CDW won 1,117 of those awards between them, accounting for one in every seven.

The £91bn, meanwhile, overstates the flow of work. More than half of it sits in framework ceilings and awards whose supplier names are withheld on security grounds. Barely one award in 14 was flagged as openly advertised.

That is according to data from Contracked, compiled from Find a Tender and Contracts Finder award notices covering the 12 months to 31 August 2026 and analysed by Computer Weekly.

The year’s IT buying ran through a handful of resellers, on a base of small awards, with most of the money concentrated in a few framework ceilings.

TL;DR – UK public sector IT buying, the year to August 2026

  • 7,994 IT contracts were awarded, worth a combined £91bn.
  • More than half the total sits in framework ceilings and withheld-supplier awards, and the typical award is worth £164,000.
  • Five resellers won 1,117 awards (14%), Softcat alone taking 473.
  • Direct hyperscaler awards were tiny, at 44 awards worth £531m.
  • Where buyers advertised openly, the median was five bids, and 42 (10%) drew a single bid.
  • 1,812 contracts end within 12 months, 1,160 within six.

    The money, and what inflates it

    The £91bn total needs reading with care. Contracked flags 153 of the 7,994 awards as frameworks, withheld-supplier deals or multi-supplier panels, and those rows carry £55.5bn between them – more than half the total. The framework ceilings alone are enormous: Technology Services 4 carries £16bn, G-Cloud 15 £14bn, and Digital Outcomes and Specialists 7 £12bn. These are maximum values shared across every supplier on the framework, not money spent in the year. Strip the 153 rows out, and the remaining 7,841 awards are worth £35.5bn, with a median of £164,000.

    By category, IT services led the year at £27bn, ahead of hardware at £16.7bn and software packages at £15.8bn. On the buyer side, the two framework-owning bodies dominate: the Crown Commercial Service (CCS) and the Government Commercial Agency (GCA) account for more than £50bn of published value between them, most of it framework ceilings, with the Ministry of Defence next at £15.2bn.

    The biggest buyers

    Biggest by published value, September 2025 to August 2026:

    • Crown Commercial Service – £28.8bn (framework ceilings) 
    • Government Commercial Agency – £22bn (framework ceilings) 
    • Ministry of Defence – £15.2bn 
    • HM Revenue & Customs – £4.5bn 
    • NHS Shared Business Services – £2.9bn (framework ceilings) 
    • Transport for London – £2bn 
    • Home Office – £1.3bn 
    • Ministry of Justice – £1bn

    Most active by number of awards:

    • Ministry of Defence – 214
    • UK Shared Business Services – 157
    • Home Office – 138
    • HM Revenue & Customs – 121
    • NHS England – 103

    Source: Contracked.io | Analysis: Computer Weekly

    The framework spikes show up clearly month by month, sitting on top of a steadier base of ordinary awards.

    G-Cloud 15 is the clearest example of how a ceiling distorts the picture. The GCA estimates about £3bn a year will pass through the framework, but it carries a £14bn headline across four years. The GCA says about 90% of the suppliers awarded places are small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), although a place on the framework does not guarantee any business, and the framework has faced criticism over supplier requirements that smaller firms argue shut them out.

    Who wins?

    By volume, the work runs through a small group of resellers. Softcat won 473 awards across 238 different buyers, followed by Phoenix Software with 231, Insight Direct with 163, Civica with 136 and CDW with 114.

    The five together took 14% of every award made in the year. Softcat, the UK’s largest Microsoft partner, is the pattern in miniature. AwardedTenders, which tracks public procurement, counted it winning work from 217 public buyers in 2025, against just 19 each for Microsoft and Oracle, whose licences Softcat resells. The suppliers sell through the channel, not to the buyer.

    By value, the picture flips. IBM took £13.1bn, almost all of it through the £12.4bn Defence Equipment Engineering Asset Management Service (DEEAMS) contract for the Ministry of Defence. Indra took £1.96bn from Transport for London, and Capgemini £1.51bn. A further £36.7bn of awards carry supplier names withheld on security grounds.

    The hyperscalers themselves barely appear. Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft and Google Cloud won 44 awards between them, worth £531m, the largest being a £394m deal for HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) to exit three Fujitsu-run datacentres. Computer Weekly reported that AWS emerged as the sole bidder after rivals exited. The resellers, by contrast, took 1,693 awards worth £2.09bn, and they sit at the centre of the public sector procurement story.

    The competition picture

    Competition is harder to read. Contracked flags only 591 awards (7.4%) as openly advertised, and just 417 of those publish a bid count. Where buyers do advertise and report, competition looks healthy, with a median of five bids, 80 awards drawing 10 or more, and single-bidder awards the exception at 42, or 10%.

    Small firms feature when competition is real. Across the 394 awards that report a bid count and the share from SMEs, 57.8% of bids came from SMEs.

    For the other 92.6% of awards, the notices do not record the procurement route, so no one outside the buyer can see whether competition happened. That opacity matters because so much of the spend is software licensing, with the Competition and Markets Authority to decide whether to give Microsoft strategic market status by February 2027.

    The renewal wave

    Much of this is about to come back to market. Some 1,812 of the contracts end within the next 12 months, 1,160 of them within six, so the buyers who awarded them will decide again soon. After the period covered here, HMRC awarded Salesforce a £2bn contract for its customer relationship management platform on 30 September 2026.

    The renewal wave is where the lopsided market bites. If a handful of resellers keep winning one award in seven and most of the rest is not flagged as openly advertised, the buyers returning to market next year will meet the same channel, and the same few firms, as last year.

title: UK government adapts Post Office scandal redress schemes and investigates pre-Horizon software
raw_text:
The UK government has launched an investigation into software used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon system was rolled out, and has opened up new routes to compensation for scandal victims.

Despite compensation of over £1.7bn being paid to more than 14,000 victims of the Post Office scandal in Horizon redress schemes, there are claims of remaining unfairness and people being left out.

Furthermore, the government is launching a new investigation into pre-Horizon software and the impact of its errors. This includes the Capture system, which, like Horizon, led to unexplained losses and destroyed lives, including subpostmasters being convicted of crimes based on its data.

“To ensure no stone is left unturned in uncovering the full extent of issues affecting subpostmasters, a new independent investigation into software used before Horizon has also now been confirmed,” the government said.

There has already been an independent investigation into Capture by forensic experts at Kroll, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” the Post Office software had caused accounting losses, but a new investigation could look deeper at the problems it caused.

Other systems such as ECCO+ have been pointed to as error-prone and likely to cause unexplained shortfalls that subpostmasters were forced to pay for, but beyond Computer Weekly investigations and work by campaigner Rupert Lloyd Thomas and the National Federation of Subpostmasters, little has been done to support affected users.

Read more about the Post Office’s ECCO+ software

  • Federation requests government investigation into third Post Office branch system.
  • Government looking into third faulty Post Office IT system.
  • Post Office Capture and Ecco+ users asked to make contact with Scottish statutory body.
  • Minister asks for evidence of Post Office ECCO+ system problems.
  • Email from 1999 reveals Post Office ECCO+ system crash problems.
  • Post Office acknowledges ECCO+ user’s calls for help three decades ago.

    New redress paths

    On financial redress, the government said it has introduced “a new package of measures to provide pathways to conclusion for schemes, strengthen scrutiny and fairness, and investigate pre-Horizon software”.

    New deadlines have been set for applications to a scheme for former users of the Post Office’s Capture system, which will now close on 31 March 2027, and a redress scheme for those wrongly convicted of crimes based on evidence from Horizon, which will close to new submissions on 27 July 2027.

    Over £9m has so far been paid to claimants through the Capture redress scheme, but claimants believe the sums they received fall well short. Earlier this month, Computer Weekly revealed that the husband of a former subpostmaster and Capture user, who had her financial and mental health destroyed at the hands of the Post Office, is preparing a judicial review to challenge the government’s financial redress decision.

    Ken Tooby warned the government that he will apply for judicial review of the decision to award him less than a third of a claim submitted on behalf of his late wife, June Tooby, who was blamed for losses recorded on the organisation’s faulty Capture software.

    As reported previously by Computer Weekly, another former subpostmaster, Lee Bowerman, received a financial settlement offer through the Capture redress scheme that equated to just 7% of his professionally calculated claim.

    Bowerman, who lost his business in South Wales more than 30 years ago, was part of a group that helped the government design the scheme.

    He complained that consequential losses were not included in the offer and that there was limited opportunity to appeal decisions on redress awards. He called for parity with former Horizon users, who were also affected in the Post Office scandal.

    The Horizon Shortfalls Scheme (HSS) is also being changed, with a new independent review process being introduced for subpostmasters who were previously told that there is insufficient evidence to receive a fixed sum offer of compensation.

    A new independent review process will also open next month for people who accepted HSS fixed sum offers and believe their claims were undervalued. 

    Following the latest government announcement, Post Office minister Kate Dearden said: “We must never lose sight of the suffering caused by the Horizon and Capture scandals. Behind every pound of compensation paid is a person whose life has been turned upside down by the scandal.

    “We remain unwavering in our commitment to provide fair, comprehensive and timely redress to all those affected and ensure that a scandal like this never happens again.” Registration remains open for the Horizon Family Members Redress Scheme, with claims processing expected to begin early next year.

summary:
The UK government has launched an investigation into software used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon system was rolled out, and has opened up new routes to compensation for scandal victims.

Despite compensation of over £1.7bn being paid to more than 14,000 victims of the Post Office scandal in Horizon redress schemes, there are claims of remaining unfairness and people being left out.

Furthermore, the government is launching a new investigation into pre-Horizon software and the impact of its errors. This includes the Capture system, which, like Horizon, led to unexplained losses and destroyed lives, including subpostmasters being convicted of crimes based on its data.

“To ensure no stone is left unturned in uncovering the full extent of issues affecting subpostmasters, a new independent investigation into software used before Horizon has also now been confirmed,” the government said.

There has already been an independent investigation into Capture by forensic experts at Kroll, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” the Post Office software had caused accounting losses, but a new investigation could look deeper at the problems it caused.

Other systems such as ECCO+ have been pointed to as error-prone and likely to cause unexplained shortfalls that subpostmasters were forced to pay for, but beyond Computer Weekly investigations and work by campaigner Rupert Lloyd Thomas and the National Federation of Subpostmasters, little has been done to support affected users.

    New redress paths

    On financial redress, the government said it has introduced “a new package of measures to provide pathways to conclusion for schemes, strengthen scrutiny and fairness, and investigate pre-Horizon software”.

    New deadlines have been set for applications to a scheme for former users of the Post Office’s Capture system, which will now close on 31 March 2027, and a redress scheme for those wrongly convicted of crimes based on evidence from Horizon, which will close to new submissions on 27 July 2027.

    Over £9m has so far been paid to claimants through the Capture redress scheme, but claimants believe the sums they received fall well short. Earlier this month, Computer Weekly revealed that the husband of a former subpostmaster and Capture user, who had her financial and mental health destroyed at the hands of the Post Office, is preparing a judicial review to challenge the government’s financial redress decision.

    Ken Tooby warned the government that he will apply for judicial review of the decision to award him less than a third of a claim submitted on behalf of his late wife, June Tooby, who was blamed for losses recorded on the organisation’s faulty Capture software.

    As reported previously by Computer Weekly, another former subpostmaster, Lee Bowerman, received a financial settlement offer through the Capture redress scheme that equated to just 7% of his professionally calculated claim.

    Bowerman, who lost his business in South Wales more than 30 years ago, was part of a group that helped the government design the scheme.

    He complained that consequential losses were not included in the offer and that there was limited opportunity to appeal decisions on redress awards. He called for parity with former Horizon users, who were also affected in the Post Office scandal.

    The Horizon Shortfalls Scheme (HSS) is also being changed, with a new independent review process being introduced for subpostmasters who were previously told that there is insufficient evidence to receive a fixed sum offer of compensation.

    A new independent review process will also open next month for people who accepted HSS fixed sum offers and believe their claims were undervalued. 

    Following the latest government announcement, Post Office minister Kate Dearden said: “We must never lose sight of the suffering caused by the Horizon and Capture scandals.

title: Capita postpones investor event to focus on CSPS fix
raw_text:
Capita cannot hold an event for shareholders, investors and market watchers because it wants to focus on fixing the botched administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS).

The troubled scheme has already reduced the firm’s profits by £40m.

The outsourcer said its Capital Market Event, planned for 4 November, had been postponed to enable it to “focus on improving the service delivery on the Civil Service Pension Scheme contract”.

It said it will include an update when it announces its trading statement next month. “Alongside its regular trading update in December, Capita will provide a comprehensive update, including detail on the group’s new operational segments following completion of the disposal of the private sector contact centre business,” said a company statement.

It added that it is making good operational progress with the CSPS contract. “This includes the roll-out of new features and further planned upgrades, such as the launch of the retirement modelling tool, which is due to go live in the coming weeks,” it said.

“Capita recognises further improvement in service is required, and we are implementing further automation and strengthening governance, including improved management information.”

Alongside the  Cabinet Office, it said it is working on a comprehensive recovery plan, “focusing on improving member experience and delivering operational stability”.

Pension disaster

In 2023, the Cabinet Office awarded Capita a seven-year contract worth £239m for the administration of the CSPS, which has 1.7 million members. The takeover from the previous administrator, MyCSP, took place on 1 December 2025. 

Since it took on the contract, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises, leaving claimants in severe financial difficulties. Thousands of retired civil servants are affected by the CSPS problems – some have waited nearly a year for their pensions, and at least one has been forced to use a food bank.

Capita has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure mounting on the organisation, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

In January 2026, just a month after Capita took over from MyCSP and following a litany of problems, a troubleshooter stepped in from HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) to lead an “urgent recovery plan”, which included 150 staff being moved temporarily from HMRC to the service.

Disaster after disaster has now prompted the government to make the decision to bring the service in-house, but no timeline has been given.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson recently told Computer Weekly that the government is “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring the pension scheme back in-house” – a statement repeated by Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson.

What is now clear is that the government won’t let Capita flee without fixing a scheme it will inevitably lose. In the debate, Jameson declared her support for the government’s plan for the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, but made clear that Capita cannot just walk away, leaving a mess.

“I want Capita to pay for their mistakes, not the taxpayers to pay for their mistakes. They don’t get to just walk away and do nothing about it,” she told MPs. “They need to pay for this, they need to get everyone their pensions, and then we’ll look at what needs to be done in terms of the viability of the scheme long term.”

Civil servant campaign groups are demanding the scheme is fixed before the government makes a decision about its future.

title: ClickFix scams pose growing risk to education sector, Jisc says
raw_text:
As the Fresher’s Week hangovers fade and students across country turn their focus to the new academic year, so-called ClickFix social engineering scams targeting Britain’s higher education sector are kicking into high gear, according to academic IT and network services provider Jisc.

Amid the customary annual surge in phishing expeditions, Jisc said it is tracking a large number of ClickFix scams through its security operations sector (SOC) and cyber security incident response team (CSIRT)

ClickFix scams work by convincing users to copy, paste and run a certain set of commands on their system, usually to address and resolve a supposed technical issue. In doing so, they in fact run malicious applications that give threat actors access to the underlying network.

The organisation claims it has blocked between 300 and 37,000 phishing attacks every week against British colleges, research bodies and universities since the start of the current academic year – many of these emails will have been the precursor to a ClickFix scam.

 “Cyber criminals are constantly innovating new ways to gain access to networks. All organisations should ensure that employees and students are aware of ClickFix scams, and that no legitimate Catcha or verification check will ask users to copy, paste and run commands,” said Jisc head of security intelligence and capability, Nicole Stewart.

According to recent Microsoft disclosures, ClickFix attack volumes spiked more than 20 times between December 2025 and May 2026, with malware payloads following 96% of the time. Between February and May of this year, ClickFix user-pasted command execution was observed on over a million unique devices.

Multiple threat actors are known to leverage the ClickFix technique, which has proved highly effective since it bypasses most technical security measures.

The most prolific proponents of ClickFix attacks use them to deliver infostealers, such as LummaStealer – in the education sector such tools would be used to target research data for exfiltration, potentially by nation-state actors.

However, other threat actors have been observed using ClickFix attacks to deliver remote access trojans (Rats) such as Xworm, AsyncRAT, NetSupport and SectopRAT for hands-on keyboard activity, loaders suh as Latrodectus and MintsLoader to deliver additional malware and payloads, and even rootkits to allow their users to establish long-term persistence.

Microsoft said it has seen 23-fold growth in ClickFix volumes between December 2025 and May 2026, with malware payloads following 96% of the time while between February and May of this year, ClickFix user-pasted command execution was observed on over a million unique devices.

Jisc noted that some ClickFix scams now also store their malicious payloads on blockchain smart contracts instead of the threat actors’ own servers, which makes it considerably harder

Some variants are now also able to exploit the WebRTC standard for browser-based video calls and peer-to-peer data transfers, opening up a new avenue of attack.

Meanwhile, according to Microsoft, artificial intelligence (AI) techniques are now being used to manufacture ClickFix lures at scale – one  2025 campaign spread ClickFix activation steps via AI videos on TikTok, some of which were viewed more than half a million times.

Next steps

For defenders, prioritising user awareness and equipping people with the knowledge to identify and ward off social engineering attacks should be the first and most effective line of defence.

In particular, users should be made aware that legitimate websites or update tools will never ask them to copy and run code through the clipboard themselves. Any such prompts should be treated with extreme caution and IT security teams notified for assistance.

This said, acknowledging that even the most security-conscious people make mistakes from time to time, there are some technical steps that security teams can take to reduce the likelihood of an attempted ClickFix attack becoming a full-blown incident.

As a first step, security teams should enable browser-layer security protections wherever possible, and clamp down on user access to the Windows Run dialogue, PowerShell, or other living-off-the-land binaries (LoLbins). Where possible, endpoint telemetry should also be monitored to detect any process creation events launched via the clipboard feature.

title: PAC warns that UKRI is not delivering value for money
raw_text:
The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) and UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) are spending £9.2bn of taxpayers’ money on UK innovation. But, according to a report from the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), they need to do more to get better value for taxpayers from the UK government’s investments in research and development, and to keep the UK at the global forefront of innovation.

While the PAC noted that BIST has recently changed its procurement approach to make it more likely that UK companies will supply some of the £400m worth of specialised artificial intelligence (AI) chips it plans to purchase, the authors of the report said that British companies still find it much harder than their US counterparts to obtain the capital investment they need to grow while remaining based in the UK.

The report criticised UKRI for taking too cautious an approach when dealing with intellectual property. UKRI aims to strike a balance with the design of its IP controls so as not to inhibit companies’ growth. The PAC said that the more liberal approach to IP controls taken by UKRI, compared to other parts of the public sector, does not go far enough and BIST should go further to recover taxpayers’ money. The PAC suggest UKRI could, for example, look to take more equity stakes where it is providing funding.

Geoffrey Clifton-Brown MP, chair of the Public Accounts Committee, said: “It may strike followers of this committee’s work that our call for government to take a less cautious approach to taking a direct stake in British innovation is an unusual one. But we are a body dedicated to value for taxpayers’ money, not hoarding it. The nations currently leading the global tech race did not achieve their positions by avoiding more entrepreneurial policies. This is a simple case for the government of nothing ventured, nothing gained.”

The PAC was also critical of UKRI’s approach to cancelling projects it had already funded. In the report, the PAC said that UKRI cancelled funding for its airborne laboratory five years after deciding to upgrade it, having spent £46m of the £49m budget.

“We believe it could have taken action sooner. UKRI could also have been quicker to realise the Science and Facilities Technology Council’s (STFC’s) plans were unaffordable,” the report’s authors said. “The decisions it will soon take to bring spending back under control could have serious consequences for the UK’s skills base, for sites such as the Daresbury research campus, and for the UK’s reputation as a partner in international collaborations such as CERN.”

Another area of concern raised by the PAC is UKRI’s ability to maintain and upgrade infrastructure needed to support research. It reported that restoring university-owned research infrastructure to a fully operational condition would cost £5.6bn, at a time when many universities have large financial deficits. 

In the report, the PAC noted that BIST and UKRI failed to ensure the Archer2 national supercomputer’s replacement would be ready before Archer2 is turned off. The PAC said the 13-month expected delay would have been longer without the University of Edinburgh’s decision to proactively prepare its site by upgrading a grid connection.

Looking at regional differences, the PAC found that the current VAT framework for research infrastructure, along with other barriers, discourages researchers from using facilities outside their own institution.

“We also heard that UKRI has focused on large investments and paid less attention to whether the overall landscape is balanced, efficient and resilient,” it noted.

Clifton-Brown added: “Our report also identifies a continuing and unacceptable regional divide in researchers’ experiences outside of London and the South East. UKRI’s spending in the North seems to be going in the right direction, but without a dedicated focus on rebalancing the scales, there is every possibility of slipping back to the previous status quo.”
